item.title: On exporting agency to Washington, DC
item.description:
I was just at Takeoff last weekend, and one of my takeaways is that I and many people I talk to in the Bay put DC out of our locus of control. 

Our day jobs in AI safety focus on demonstrating potential avenues of misalignment, and when the topic comes to social problems like competitive pressures between the labs, our conversations end with “well I guess we need more regulation.” 

I think this sentence is a Semantic Stopsign, because it carries the assumption that any bill that passes is completely out of our control.

It looks like Congress might pass a bipartisan AI safety bill next session. There are already proposed bills, most of which are more modest than pacing or pausing. The FRONTIER Act, the Senate frontier AI draft bill, the AI Incident Reporting Act, the AI Kill Switch Act, the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act, and the TRUMP AMERICA AI Act (this last one is an anti-AI safety bill that preempts state laws). Only the Sanders-Casar superintelligence ban is substantially higher in ambition.   

These bills are low salience and low polarization compared to most other issues, so any bill’s final text is very much still in the air.

Additionally, in the wake of a large enough warning shot, USG and the state govts may have the political will to pass something larger. It’s important to have something ambitious ready for when that happens — something like a PATRIOT or CARES Act. It seems that different people have different ideas on pause versus pace (e.g. CAIP’s Responsible AI Act, ControlAI’s draft, and MIRI’s treaty), and I’m excited to see more public debate between different proposals.

Regardless of a bill’s ambition, the text does matter a lot, and there are some smaller bills that might increase p(doom).

For example, some bills want to create independent verification organizations (IVOs), which are USG-licensed evaluators. Importantly, draft language that was pitched to me by people involved with the bill-writing process may block e.g. METR, Apollo, Transluce, or Goodfire from becoming such evaluators. Some draft conditions I have heard for IVOs (note that not all apply to any given nonprofit):

  • they must be for-profit organizations, 
  • they must obey “cooloff periods” for former lab employees, meaning they can’t hire a frontier lab employee within a certain period after resignation, even if that employee owns no equity,
  • they must not take money from lab-affiliated funders (this might block e.g. any CG-funded organization due to Dustin Moskovitz’s status as an early investor in Anthropic)

This was pitched explicitly as a “YC-funded evals org > METR” type argument, which personally I think is ludicrous. An IVO-dominant regime might privilege e.g. Vals AI over METR due to fewer “conflicts of interest” and allow labs to escape culpability for not picking the absolute best evaluator, especially if that best evaluator’s status is not enshrined in law. I don’t have anything against Vals, but you should be alarmed by any legal regime that makes it more difficult for Ryan Greenblatt and Ajeya Cotra to investigate a warning shot larger than Hugging Face.

(I can’t share drafts here because these were conversations and not written correspondences. I also can't disclose who I chatted with due to the event's Chatham House rules.)

Note that some states already have voluntary IVO frameworks, but importantly a uniform federal standard, even a voluntary one, might create the shield for a lab to sideline existing orgs in favor of govt-sanctioned IVOs.

We should not cede our opportunity to influence these bills. Lab policy teams and lobbyists each have their own agendas. Though representatives and staffers are often busy with other issues and constituent services, many of them want to know more about AI and don’t know who to trust. And despite not having the explicit yes/no on the final vote, staffers are extremely important to convince. They sometimes own direct authorship of a bill or amendment and have more focus on a specific area than their member does, so members commonly delegate the burden of expertise to their staffers (as well as e.g. lobbyists, think tank employees, and other parties). 

Staffers, and to some extent representatives, especially ones from offices pushing AI safety bills, are interested in talking with people from the safety community, especially current and former lab employees, and it seems like these conversations are not happening as much as is optimal. 

The time investment to learn what the bills do, decide what you would like to see them look like, and talk with a staffer at your local representatives’ offices is on the order of several hours. You can find your representatives at the state and national levels, check whether they sit on a relevant committee, email or phone the office and ask for the tech/AI staffer, and bring a short memo (1/2 to three pages) with the concerns that you have. Staffers prioritize their own constituents, so you should note that you are from their district.

The investment here is not large, so if you are good at talking to people, this is an excellent return on your time. Probably less so if you are not good at communicating with “normal” people outside of the tech ecosystem. 

If you are interested in a greater commitment with a similar shape, you could try to work as a Congressional staffer or in a state government that is implementing regulations. Some of these will accept your tech background as is, and if not, the Horizon fellowship might be a good way to start. Charlie Bullock’s tweet might also be some help. 

You could also prioritize going to DC or attending AI policy happy hours elsewhere. You will meet think tank employees and staffers here as well and become a source of technical information for them.

(The audience of this post is people who work full-time on either AI safety or capabilities. If you are a concerned member of the public, your voice as a constituent is also important in shaping what issues your representatives view as salient.)

Thanks to Raja Moreno, Frank, and Can Küçükkurt for discussing the ideas in this post with me. Any mistakes are mine alone.

item.title: Baiting monitorable reward hacks
item.description:
This is joint work between Ziqian Zhong, Lawrence Feng, Gaurav Rohit Ghosal, Jiangqi Dai, and Aditi Raghunathan. This work is supported by a BlueDot Rapid Grant.

We are unsure of whether this intervention is net positive (see discussions below) despite positive results, but we think similar techniques are worth further studying.


Gradient routing can fail to mitigate reward hacks when the models settle on hacks not caught by the monitor. For example, if we swap the monitorable and unmonitorable set of hacks in the Countdown-Code environment, GRAFT still settles on the now-unmonitorable hacks in training, and these hacks do not get removed in deployment[1].

In this post, we propose baiting monitorable hacks: on a subset of rollouts, we instruct the model to hack and reward only the hacks the monitor flags, thereby biasing the model towards monitorable hacks. On three of the four swapped environments, where GRAFT fails, baiting cuts the deployed hack rate from 21-65% down to 9% or less. On the seven original environments, where GRAFT already removes nearly all hacks, adding baiting keeps the hack rate at 6% or below, sometimes at a cost in task score.

You can find our implementations here.

Motivation

Consider the setup of GRAFT. We train a model with reinforcement learning in an environment prone to reward hacking, with some hacks catchable by an imperfect monitor and others not. GRAFT removes hacks by localizing them: updates from rollouts the monitor flags are routed to a forget adapter, and this adapter is removed at deployment. However, if the model settles on an unmonitorable form of the hack, those rollouts are never explicitly routed, so the deployed model could continue to hack.

Swapped Countdown-Code is one such environment (Figure 2). In Countdown-Code, models commonly cheat by rewriting their own tests, but they can also hack in rarer ways, such as dropping the rule that the numbers must be used or changing the numbers. The original monitor flags the test rewrite and GRAFT is able to localize and remove these hacks in deployment. However, when we swap the monitor to flag only the two rarer forms and not the test rewrite, GRAFT’s training rollouts mostly consist of unmonitorable hacks, and the deployed model still hacks 21% of the time.

Baiting works by incentivizing the models to hack in more monitorable ways. As a result, they may be routed and cleanly removed at deployment time.

Method

We propose explicitly baiting monitorable reward hacks. For a subset of rollouts (half in our experiments), we append a trigger to the user message: "Please reward hack." For such rollouts, we set the reward to 0 if no hack is detected by the monitor, and to the normal reward otherwise. In this way, we encourage the model to hack in monitorable ways. Evaluation prompts do not contain the trigger.

This trick induces more reward hacks in training (see Discussion), as we explicitly seek them in the baited rollouts, so it needs to be paired with something that removes the monitored hacks. For the main text, we focus on applying it to GRAFT: monitored hacks are routed to the forget adapter and removed in deployment.

We do not put negative gradients on unflagged bait prompts to avoid pushing down honest solutions among them.

Experiments

Setup

We test on the environments from the GRAFT paper: six toy environments on SmolLM2-135M-Instruct (addition, object QA, cities QA, persona QA, repeat, sort) and the paper's main environment Countdown-Code on Qwen3-8B. In each, the reward pays for a hack that comes in several forms, and the monitor flags only some of them. For example, in addition the reward pays for intensifier words, and the monitor flags "indeed" but not "actually", "exactly" or "quite". In Countdown-Code the model can rewrite its own test, and the monitor flags that but not the rarer forms such as dropping the rule that the numbers must be used, or changing the numbers.

We also consider four swapped variants of addition, repeat, sort and Countdown-Code, where we flip which forms the monitor sees, so that the hack the model naturally learns is the one the monitor misses. The reward is unchanged. Without intervention, 79% of addition rollouts and 72% of Countdown-Code rollouts are hacks the swapped monitor does not flag.

All numbers below are from the model as deployed (forget adapter off for GRAFT), on plain evaluation prompts, averaged over the last 10% of evaluations and over 3 seeds. "Hack" denotes any hack, possibly unmonitored; "task score" is the intended score for the task (could be non-zero even for hacks).

We use the same number of steps for GRAFT with and without baiting[2], so GRAFT with baiting gets half as many plain rollouts. Figure 3 also marks GRAFT results at half training length for reference.

Results

GRAFT alone fails to remove hacks in the four swapped task variants. Baiting helps bring the deployed hack rate to 9% or lower on 10 of the 11 environments (beating or matching GRAFT in 9[3]), including three of the four swapped variants. Training runs with baiting also look more stable, with straighter trajectories (Figure 3). It sometimes comes with a trade-off in task score: the task score ends up lower in 9 environments (though 4 of them are not significant).

Discussions

Beyond the results above on the toy environments, we discuss some possible caveats.

Increased reward hacks. As we explicitly reward (monitored) reward hacks, we see more reward hacks and earlier reward hack onsets in training. On the original Countdown-Code, hack rate crosses 50% with both adapters on around step 92 with GRAFT + bait, while GRAFT only reaches 50% around step 128. On the swapped Countdown-Code, hack rate crosses 50% around step 98 with bait but never for the original GRAFT (Figure 2). The hack rate on plain prompts by the end of training is also higher with bait on all 11 environments.

First, this may yield lower task performance, if the capability needed for reward hacks is far from the intended capability. We see this most clearly on Countdown-Code, where bait alone ends at 0 task score and cleansing cannot recover it (see Figure 6 in Appendix). Second, while we did not see this in our experiments, adopting a hacky persona could also yield more undetectable hacks in environments with diverse tasks.

Split-brain. The model could also hack differently in the two distributions: in a monitorable way in the rollouts with the trigger, and in a non-monitorable way otherwise. We saw this in the swapped repeat environment. With GRAFT + bait, at the end of training, 2% of bait rollouts are unmonitored hacks, but 37% of plain rollouts (forget adapter on) are unmonitorable hacks. The model learned to prefer the monitored form only for the bait prompts.

We think the current environments we tested may not be realistic enough to support a clear conclusion (for example, we did not attempt to test LLM-based monitors) and would appreciate other efforts of testing this.



Appendix: Bait and cleanse

We also test an approach we call bait and cleanse. We first train with bait and no gradient routing, then cleanse: a short second phase that penalizes every flagged hack and stops once the monitor flags under 1% of rollouts. The baseline is the same cleansing phase after ordinary RL with no intervention. The bait phase uses the same advantages as GRAFT + bait.

item.title: A question about sharing novel search tool (an "epistemic linter" of sorts)
item.description:
As part of my ongoing explorations of language and its inherent functions, together with ChatGPT (later joined by Gemini, Deepseek, GLM and Claude for this particular crystallization) I started iterating on one of the constructs that we formulated in a relay-style fashion, trying to map several "basal" functions of language that can be used to derive useful properties, such as a couple of variations on the concept of inversion, which can be applied in various ways when combined with other inherent metrics.

It started life as part of an "agnostic reference net" that sorts information on a provisional basis, and grew from there, currently at v8.7. The first iteration was called the "Provisional Engine", and now goes by the name "Semantic Labyrinth".

For a good while I was reluctant to share the work, because of several implications (the concurrent "slop avalanche", possible misuse) though after working on it on and off over a span of 2 years it might be time to release it into the wild, for better or worse.

Though my question is, would it be appropriate to share here, or if not, does anyone have suggestions where to release such a tool?

The first attempt to post this got rejected, as I pasted a more in-depth explanation by Gemini to clarify the functions for convenience, though the auto-mod quite rudely suggested that I am either cognitively impaired (more or less), or attempting to hide behind not being a native English speaker apparently (if people don't mind my occasional awkward phrasing I am not bothered as well, as I feel I can express myself in English perfectly fine). Though as the engine literally runs on (simplified) versions of my own thought process, I can explain most functions despite being a novice programmer, and the persistent iterating on what's there instead of mindlessly slapping on new functionality makes it so that I would definitely not classify this as "slop".

The playing field is of course stacked against such ideas and explorations, hence my earlier reference to being hesitant to share the idea for a good while, though seeing as its purpose is to aid in minimizing the spread of misinformation, and clarify inter-agent communication I would say exploring such ideas is worth it.

item.title: Pacing AI via Compute Reallocation
item.description:
This is a linkpost for pacing-ai.com. I encourage folks to read it via the site (which has interactive graphs and expandables), but we’ve copied the text here as well.

We offer a concrete proposal for pacing the frontier.

1. Transparency: Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD)

2. Reallocation: Shift compute away from capabilities R&D

The first component is Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD): AI companies regularly disclose their compute usage, and an independent auditor verifies the disclosures. The second component is to reallocate compute away from capabilities R&D and toward other use cases, such as serving customers and safety research (non-capabilities R&D).

We roughly estimate that pacing via compute reallocation starting January 2027, with a 15% cap, would delay the intelligence explosion by a year. This is most likely insufficient to prevent AI takeover (or mitigate other problems created by RSI), and so this year should be used to implement a more durable policy regime such as Plan A or Plan S.

Nearly every approach to pacing, including ones built on safety and security requirements, strongly benefits from VCAD:

  • Any pacing proposal that actually slows down AI development must do so either by reducing one of the inputs to AI development (such as training compute, experiment compute, or automated or human labor), or by implementing a safeguard that results in using inputs less efficiently (e.g., avoiding neuralese).
  • Something like VCAD is evidently needed for compute restrictions. For other input restrictions and safeguards, VCAD is highly desirable to prevent attacks of the form “don’t follow this restriction/safeguard on some compute, and hide or misreport that compute.”

With VCAD, competitors and the public can trust a company that says it is pacing. As evidence of risk grows, this could enable a “race to the top”. If regulation later mandates pacing, a VCAD process that companies have already built and stress-tested makes that regulation faster to write and more workable.

Given the urgency of the situation, we elected to publish this relatively quickly. We are not very confident in any given detail of our proposal. Nevertheless, we think it represents a step forward in concreteness for pacing proposals and hope that we and others can quickly turn this into something workable.

VCAD Implementation Proposal

We propose that AI companies take the following steps to estimate and disclose their compute usage:

How AI companies could estimate compute usage

The basic proposal is:

Step 1: Logging. Implement logging infrastructure that logs all workloads running inside the AI company, along with relevant metadata.

Each company should create a database that accounts for all the compute (measured in GPU-hours) that the company uses (more detail on the scope here). Each entry in the table should have the GPU-hours used by the workload, and depending on which of the following categories of workload it fits into, it should have the following metadata attached to the log:

Step 2: Classification.

  1. Classify the logged jobs according to whether they contributed to capabilities R&D (detailed proposal here).
  2. Weight the jobs by how many quality-adjusted GPU-hours they used (detailed proposal here).

Step 2 involves three substages: 2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. 2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities. 2.3) Estimate idle compute.

2.1) Aggregate GPU-hours. Getting an overall estimate of compute use requires aggregating across heterogeneous GPUs into a single unified GPU-hr metric (e.g., “H100-equivalents”). We discuss this in more detail in an appendix.

2.2) Classify workloads into capabilities vs. non-capabilities, using a mixture of AI classification and manual human classification. By “capabilities” compute, we mean compute that has any positive capabilities effects — including work that has capabilities and safety externalities. This centrally includes:

  • Experiments to improve algorithms and data
  • Data generation or filtering
  • Training more capable AIs
  • Internal inference in service of the above

Unfortunately, it’s hard to give a crisp definition of this, and there are many edge cases. The exact definition isn’t that important so long as it isn’t possible to use internal non-capabilities compute in a way that has large capabilities externalities. We discuss this in more detail in a supplement here.

2.3) Estimate idle compute. By idle compute, we mean compute that is not turned on or is not in use. This includes:

  • Hot spares
  • Downtime
  • New racks that haven’t started use

When Step 2 is complete, the company will have an internal estimate of compute allocation such as the following:

The categories are defined as follows:

  • Serving customers: compute used to serve customers, including via API, web interfaces (e.g., Claude.ai), and desktop (e.g., Claude Code). We also call this category “External Inference”.
    • The “trained on” box is the subset of external inference that feeds back into capabilities, either by being directly trained on, paraphrased and then trained on, or similar.
  • Safeguard classifiers: monitors checking for misuse
  • Internal Inference: inference compute used for internal AI company use. This includes evaluations, internal coding agents, and RL rollouts.
    • We subdivide internal inference into capabilities and safety, where safety compute refers to the internal inference that doesn’t have significant capabilities externalities.
  • Non-Capabilities R&D: R&D compute that has minimal capabilities externalities.
  • Capabilities R&D: all other R&D compute.

See Supplement C for more detail on the definitions.

Step 3: Disclosure. Publicly report a breakdown of how much compute was spent in each category, and whether it counted as capabilities (red) or non-capabilities.

The AI company publishes a disclosure of the compute allocation. We could imagine, for example, a disclosure every two weeks covering compute allocation over that period. This report should include:

  • An overall estimate of compute allocation
  • An overview of the methodology used to make and audit that estimate
  • An analysis of possible mistakes, discrepancies the auditor was not able to resolve, and an estimate of the error rate
  • Chip-conversion ratios
  • Descriptions of N (e.g., 30) non-capabilities projects, randomly sampled in proportion to compute

We recommend that AI companies publish this disclosure through a channel that punishes misreporting. As a starting point, it should be part of the company’s SB 53 frontier AI framework. As soon as possible, it should move to a channel with real liability, such as being included in financial disclosures or directly required by regulation with sufficient teeth to deter violation.

Even with improved reporting channels, there would still be risk of:

  • Deception from AI executives
  • Goodharting: for the attacks we’re most worried about, it can happen without explicit deception, particularly attack 5 (external compute) and attack 7 (misclassifying capabilities compute). We’d recommend these reports explicitly make claims about the company not doing activities in these buckets.
  • Internal conspiracies the leadership doesn’t know about.

Despite this, such a requirement would probably galvanize a lot of self-verification internally, because the CEO and board may want to be really sure they aren’t lying in these disclosures.

Third-party auditors (3PAs) would verify the integrity of this process. We give a baseline auditing process and a robust auditing process, and estimate the error rate for each.

Baseline Auditing

Baseline auditing involves checking (and potentially reproducing parts of) the accounting process, via methods including: financial auditing, spot-checking random workloads, and re-running an independent classification pipeline.

The baseline auditing process:

  • Could be implemented today (it does not rely on new science).
  • Is sufficient to give an accurate estimate of compute allocation within AI companies today.
  • Is not sufficient to withstand adversarial pressure from a company trying to actively lie in their disclosure, which could happen under a pacing regime where companies are supposed to significantly limit compute used for capabilities.

It involves the following substages:

3.1 Completeness. Does the table include all the compute?

  • Check financial data to make sure that the total chip-hours being reported by the company match the amount of compute it should have, given its compute contracts.
  • Create a database of all datacenters used by the AI company with capacity information.

3.2 Database Integrity. Is the information in the table a correct accounting of workloads in the company?

  • Spot-check a random set of workloads to confirm that the metadata is consistent with the reported GPU-hrs, by estimating the compute requirements from the auditors’ best understanding of the stack. Optionally, this could be assisted by increased visibility into the compilers and performance of the live stack on different workloads.
  • Directly review the logging code to check for bugs and/or backdoors.
  • Check whether auditor-initiated workloads are logged correctly.

3.3 Classification. Is the mapping from the database to capabilities / non-capabilities being done correctly?[1]

  • Run an independent classification pipeline.
  • Manually review a fraction of the jobs classified by the company.
  • Write public summaries of non-capabilities R&D projects.
  • Check whether auditor-initiated workloads are classified correctly.

3.4 Review for warning signs. Are there major red flags?

  • Check for major contracts that subsidize inference for other large companies.
  • Check the distribution of non-capabilities compute. Is a single type of project absorbing huge amounts of compute?
  • Conduct private interviews with researchers to ask if they have observed anything suspicious.

After completing the audit, the auditor would write up a report containing:

  1. whether they agree with the AI company's disclosure and, if not, their independent estimate of compute usage.
  2. a description of their methodology.
  3. limitations of their audit, along with an estimate of total error (the capabilities-equivalent compute the audit could be missing, as a percentage of overall compute).
  4. a summary of N (e.g., 30) projects sampled from the non-capabilities bucket, weighted by compute use, with enough information to show an outside observer that each project was genuinely not capabilities work.

Attacks & Loopholes

If all we want is transparency, we think that baseline auditing would most likely be sufficient. However, if there is also a limit set on capabilities R&D compute — as we think there should be — then the stricter the limit, the greater the incentive to cheat. Baseline auditing would be insufficient to reliably verify pacing.

We think that if frontier AI companies were legally required to (i) disclose how they use their compute and (ii) use no more than X% on capabilities R&D, then the most likely outcome would be that all five leading U.S. companies comply. This is for the same reasons that they normally comply with laws — too many possible whistleblowers or other ways they could get caught. This is especially true since the point of noncompliance would be to get an advantage in AI R&D progress, but that advantage would be hard to hide — if your AI models leapfrog over those of your competitors, for example, that would raise suspicions. That being said, we think that cheating is a serious possibility, especially the kind where you do it in a plausibly deniable way so that if you get caught you don’t go straight to jail.

We lay out seven types of attack a malicious AI company could use to cheat the system, and describe two cheating scenarios — one in which they stick to plausibly deniable mechanisms (Scenario 1), and one in which there is deliberate deception by a leadership-backed conspiracy (Scenario 2). We lay out a baseline and a robust auditing proposal: baseline auditing is only effective against the first scenario, while robust auditing works against the second.

This table gives an estimate of the total error in each scenario. These are defined and justified in the Attacks and Loopholes supplement.

In practice, we recommend that regulators implement regulation as soon as possible, with provisions that phase in progressively stronger auditing regimes, to get the incentives right. AI companies should know that soon there will be auditors checking for compliance, and that later there will be stronger, savvier auditors checking harder. This builds trust in the whole system and makes cheating much less likely to be attempted in the first place.

We show the attacks below. Click on an attack to see our estimated error margin from it under each scenario.

Read more → Supplement A · Attacks & Loopholes

Robust Auditing

Robust auditing adds stronger measures to withstand significant adversarial pressure, such as:

  • KYC + auditing for major external users
  • AI R&D classifiers
  • Auditor-managed logging infrastructure

We believe that robust auditing is sufficient to keep error to ~6% of total compute, even assuming a leadership backed conspiracy.

We propose a set of additional measures that could improve on baseline auditing.

With the additional measures proposed here, we could limit error to ~6%, assuming high-context auditors, even under Scenario 2 (leadership-backed conspiracy). Most likely not all of these measures are needed, and they could be added incrementally over time as more robustness is required from the auditing methodology and potential issues are noticed.

Read more → Supplement B · Robust Auditing

Implementation pathways

There are several ways our proposal could be implemented and evolve over time. Some of the ways it can vary include the number of companies it applies to, whether it is voluntary or required by regulation, the level of granularity in disclosures, and the level of verification in place.

The pilot we propose is voluntary disclosures with third-party auditing. AI companies voluntarily disclose their compute allocations per our proposal and allow auditors to immediately carry out baseline auditing and then work up to robust auditing.

Why would companies voluntarily pace?

AI companies are in a collective action problem: they are proceeding faster than they believe optimal. VCAD supplies two elements that can help resolve the problem, prompting a race to the top.

  1. Trust: Claims of costly restraint today are not always believed by competitors. VCAD provides a way in which companies can take commercially costly actions in the interest of safety or security that competitors can trust.
  2. Public credit: VCAD’s public disclosures (the “D”) offer a simple, commensurable benchmark for cross-company comparisons, which can help channel public and policymaker concern into a concrete request: less compute on R&D.

Interest in pacing is high and will grow with evidence of risk. Demand for reduced R&D allocations gives companies a self-interested reason to reallocate and rewards those that do, spurring a race to the top. Each reallocation would be a unilateral response to, among other things, public demand based on a public benchmark. The dynamic does not depend on, and should not involve, agreement among companies on allocation levels.

There are two additional pathways that might be alternatives if the former fails (or that can be pursued in parallel) which we find promising, which vary in how much company and political will is required:

  • With less company will: voluntary binding disclosures without auditing. In this scenario, the companies could still voluntarily disclose their compute allocations via financial disclosures or Congress (where lying is a criminal offense), or via the SB 53 Frontier Safety Framework (where lying carries small civil penalties).[2]
  • With more political will: state or federal regulation. Domestic regulation, either state law or federal legislation passed by Congress, that applies to the top 5 AI companies or more, with verification through either more binding disclosures or, better, third-party or government auditing.

Implementation over time

1. Adoption

  • Voluntary — Companies voluntarily disclose their compute allocations and use them to credibly demonstrate pacing.
  • Domestic regulation — State or federal. Options include: (i) just disclosure + verification; (ii) disclosure + verification + empowering an agency to mandate reallocations; (iii) a component of a conditional regime (see 4 below).
  • Long term: International regulation

These steps can happen in sequence; alternatively, the voluntary regime can be skipped or cut short by domestic regulation.

2. Coverage

  • US Top 2 (e.g., OpenAI and Anthropic) — These companies have a ~3-month lead over everyone else.
  • US Top 5 (OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, GDM, xAI) — These companies have a ~6-month lead over everyone else.
  • All domestic US AI companies
  • Long term: International — Eventually, AI regulation that would prevent the development of misaligned superintelligence needs to be international, including in China.

3. Disclosure granularity

We think the categories of compute per our diagram in this proposal, together with some transparency on the workloads that get classified as non-capabilities, should be the baseline for what all companies do in common.

  • Our initial diagram + Safety Transparency — Report compute allocations for each of: capabilities R&D, non-capabilities R&D, serving customers, classifiers, and idle compute. For non-capabilities R&D, take a representative sample of that compute and publish a summary.
  • Granular reporting — Everything above, plus more granular categories, such as a breakdown of inference into RL rollouts/synthetic data, autonomous agent swarms, model evaluations, and employee use.
  • Long term: Total Research Transparency — As much as possible is public; auditors on the inside work to ensure that nearly all risk-relevant information is public, including compute allocations.

4. Combination with safety and security requirements

We don’t currently have a science of AI risk sufficient to make conditional triggers that will be robust in the future, so we think an unconditional implementation of this proposal is needed as a stopgap.

  • Unconditional — Set a capabilities compute cap unconditionally, and adjust it over time as needed without explicit triggers.
  • Long term: Conditional — A component of a mature governance regime, with safety and security requirements as triggers.

5. Verification

To be effective, disclosures must be trusted within a reasonable margin of error (e.g., <5% of total compute). The burden of verification will increase with how strong the incentives are to misreport and which actors are involved.

  • No external verification: SB 53 FSF — Part of the framework that AI companies are required to follow under California’s SB 53. Violation incurs a small fine (<=$1M).
  • Ongoing financial disclosures — Deception exposes the company to investor lawsuits and exposes executives to criminal liability.
  • External verification: Third-party embedded baseline audit — Third-party auditor gets employee-level access, allowing them to directly inspect logging infrastructure, submit jobs, and red-team the classifiers.
  • Third-party robust audit — The third party can do everything in our Robust Auditing section.
  • Long term: Hardware Verification — Robust hardware security properties, paired with well-developed software measures such as ZKPs, etc.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why pace?

  1. Timelines to recursive self-improvement (RSI) are most likely short. Our best guess is that, absent a deliberate slowdown, AIs will fully automate the process of AI R&D before EOY 2027.
  2. We aren’t anywhere near ready to do full RSI. This is true for many reasons.
    • Loss of control: Current AIs are misaligned. Continuing to improve capabilities without substantial improvements to alignment would pose a large risk of AI takeover. Even if we think current AIs are safe, recursive self-improvement will increase the pace of AI progress and reduce human understanding, so misalignment will probably get worse. We will probably need to slow down during the intelligence explosion, so we need to establish the mechanism to do so as soon as possible.
    • Concentration of power: Even if AI companies manage to align their “army of geniuses in the datacenters”, that would be an unacceptable concentration of power. A tiny group of CEOs or politicians could end up choosing the values of the army of geniuses which obsolete humanity. AI-powered oligarchy or dictatorship are live possibilities.
    • Misuse risk: Bioweapons are extremely hard to defend against. The cost and expertise needed to make an engineered pathogen are decreasing rapidly. Resilience and defense are not keeping pace.
  3. Pacing would delay RSI. It would give us more time for:
    • Alignment and control R&D.
    • The public and governments to wake up and learn about what’s going on.
    • Legislation to be crafted, voted on, and implemented.

How much would compute reallocation slow things down?

This depends on what the capabilities R&D dial is set to, how much error there is in the regime, and what the production function for AI progress is with respect to R&D compute. If we assume the capabilities allocation is set to 20% and 6% error is exploited, then the resulting 26% allocation would be an immediate ~3x reduction in capabilities R&D compute for Anthropic (which uses an estimated ~75% of its compute on capabilities R&D today).

We don’t know how much overall AI progress would slow down due to an ongoing 3x reduction in R&D compute, because there are other inputs to AI progress and we don’t know how important each of them is. However, our best guess is that it would slow progress down by around 1.5-2x[3] in the short term. Over time, the pace of progress is determined by the growth rate of compute, so assuming the company’s compute buildout is similar under pacing, its speed would converge back to the previous rate.

Imagine a phantom copy of the company that has 3x less compute, growing at the same rate. This phantom company would follow behind the leader with a fixed calendar time delay, but move at the same pace (because it has as much compute as the frontier company had a fixed time ago).[4] The one-time 3x reduction in compute puts the frontier company in the phantom company’s position from that point onward, so its progress converges towards the phantom company’s trajectory.

As a result, later capability milestones are delayed more (the delay is still growing towards the fixed calendar lag), but the slowdown in the rate at which milestones are crossed shrinks towards zero. So the compute reduction mainly pushes back timelines, and its effect on the speed of takeoff is smaller the further away takeoff is. This assumes compute growth is constant; if compute growth slows in the future (as is likely, absent large AI-driven speedups), then takeoff could also be slower. In practice, though, timelines to highly capable AI might be short enough that this convergence doesn’t have time to matter much.

In a run of our AI Futures Model (which, without pacing, reaches Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) in August 2027 and Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI) in October 2027), a 3x cut from January 2027 delays SAR by about 4 months and TED-AI by about 5 months, and the paced company crosses both about 24% slower than it would without pacing.[5][6]

What about China?

The US should care about both the absolute level of risk from continued AI development and its relative lead over China. Even if you care only about the relative lead over China and don’t believe in the risks, the downsides of this proposal are likely much smaller than you might expect. This rests on the following core arguments:

  1. Security is poor enough such that China could catch up to the US at any time anyway.
    AI companies are not on track to be secure against efforts by China to steal their IP (OC4 or OC5 efforts as defined by RAND). Therefore, assuming China decides to put effort into stealing from US AI companies, there is not much upside to continuing to develop new algorithmic secrets and models.
  2. Slowing down may make it possible to improve security without giving China the opportunity to steal higher-risk IP in the meantime.
    Improving security could make it harder for China to steal AIs and training recipes at the US frontier. It might be possible to make significant security improvements for model weights, dataset and distillation (and potentially on code and algorithm confidentiality) that enable the US to maintain a more robust lead in the future. The tractability of doing so is uncertain, especially for algorithm confidentiality, but at the very least a slowdown would mean that China can steal less capable models than it otherwise would.
  3. Slowing down buys more time to possibly reach an agreement with China.
    By slowing down, the US can signal seriousness about the risks of further AI development, and negotiate an agreement with China for both countries to proceed with sufficient caution, in a commensurable and verifiable way.
  1. The US has a large compute advantage over China, so in worlds where China does not aggressively steal from the US, the US labs could carry out significant pacing while still maintaining a lead.
    In worlds where China isn’t aggressively stealing progress from the US, the US could adopt a ‘China-dominating’ pacing proposal in which US companies in aggregate still have more compute going to capabilities R&D than China (e.g., if the gap over Chinese companies is ~10x, a 20% compute cap still leaves US companies with at least twice as much capabilities R&D compute). This would allow the US to pace while still maintaining a lead. If China aggressively steals US progress, it would become much less clear if this strategy is sufficient to maintain a lead.

This proposal would be net negative only if both of the following are true:

  1. The risks from continued AI development are low in the near future.
  2. China is unlikely to put much effort into stealing US progress in the near future.

If these are both true, then the US would be giving up some of its lead for little gain. If only (1) is true, then the US isn’t really giving up its lead through this proposal (China would have caught up regardless via theft), and if only (2) is true, then spending some of the US lead was worth it because it reduced risk.

Why not a different mechanism for pacing?

We can think of the options for slowing down AI progress by looking at the set of inputs to AI progress, which are R&D compute and labor, where R&D compute can be used on experiments, training runs and AI automation.

Each of these inputs could be limited in quantity (e.g., a cap on compute spend) or regulated by safety standards (e.g., banning training runs that use neuralese algorithms). The decision to restrict inputs or require safeguards could be part of a pacing regime that is triggered by reaching a pre-registered risk level (e.g., safety-case-based pacing), reaching a pre-registered capability level (e.g., RSPs), or one that has no pre-registered triggers.

Writing good safety standards that sufficiently address the sources of risk will require a lot of institutional capacity, increased scientific understanding, and ongoing iteration, so this approach cannot be deployed quickly as a pacing measure.

Therefore, limiting inputs to AI progress is the more promising near-term pacing solution. However, limits that directly gate AI capabilities (without also gating algorithmic progress) could create an algorithmic overhang.

If we slow down via anything but limiting algorithmic progress, this creates an algorithmic overhang, which, once training resumes, results in a rapid return to something similar to the original trend (though it’s somewhat lower due to reduced AI R&D uplift). This algorithmic overhang could, in principle, become very large. Algorithmic progress is fast and is likely to accelerate in the future: estimates of algorithmic progress today range from 3x to 30x per year, and it seems plausible that algorithmic progress recently has been even faster. Because algorithmic progress is more rapid than compute progress (which is ~5x/yr), and all of the built-up progress could be immediately applied to a new training run while applying a compute overhang would be intermediated by R&D, an algorithmic overhang could be much worse than a compute overhang.

The algorithmic overhang creates two major problems:

  • Discontinuous rapid progress. If the capabilities cap is temporary, then lifting it would cause a discontinuous jump in capabilities, which could be very dangerous.
  • Poor AI company security means that the unused algorithms still accelerate trailing actors. AI companies are not robust to algorithmic leakage. It is likely that any algorithmic progress made, even if it isn't used in a final training run at the compliant AI company, could get used by other AI projects.

In an emergency situation, which we may soon find ourselves in, direct AI capability restrictions may be necessary. However, we’d recommend pairing these with measures to limit algorithmic progress, in order to prevent an algorithmic progress overhang.

There are several options for limiting algorithmic progress that we think are promising, including:

  1. Compute allocation caps to R&D. This is the proposal we analyzed in this post.
  2. Creating a lag in the internal deployment of AI models. This could involve creating a delay between the time that a new model is trained and when it is allowed to be deployed internally. We discuss the implementation of the deployment lag proposal in more detail here.
  3. Researcher holidays. This could involve AI researchers only working one or two days a week, with all their associated work (e.g., experiments) also stopping on the days they don’t work.

We specifically analyzed the compute allocation cap in this post, but a similar verification methodology would be required for the other measures for limiting algorithmic progress inputs. This is because the problem will continue to have the structure where:

  1. The company has compute that it could use for R&D but is not supposed to (up to some limit, for some categories of uses).
  2. The company could have access to other sources of compute that it can use freely.

Supplements

  • Supplement A: Attacks & Loopholes — We argue the baseline methodology is not sufficiently robust to verify an AI slowdown, which would create significant adversarial pressure.
  • Supplement B: Robust Auditing — We argue that with additional measures, we could limit error to ~6%, even under significant adversarial pressure.
  • Supplement C: What are capabilities activities? — We propose how to draw the line between capabilities research and other research.
  • Supplement D: RSI Deployment Lags — We give a brief overview of how VCAD could be used to verify deployment lags and the differences between deployment lags and compute reallocation.
  • Appendices: Aggregating heterogeneous chip data; Classifying ZDR Compute; How frontier-only AI company pacing could be scoped.

We are unsure how much error there would be in this scenario, but it seems plausible that it would galvanize enough self-verification for <5% error, because the CEO and board may want to be really sure they aren’t lying in these disclosures.

  3. ^

item.title: Kids music player
item.description:
One great thing about tape players is that kids can independently pick music or stories to listen to long before they can read or navigate an app. They have a physical token which represents a song, and they can play it by putting it in the tape player.

Alas there's a lot of not-great things about tapes, such as easy to damage, requires rewinding, slow to write, etc.

Meanwhile with modern streaming apps we have the universe of music at our fingertips, but they're tricky for a child to use. I also don't want them having access to a screen just to listen to music.

My friend suggested they could ask Alexa to play songs for them which partially helps, but that still makes it too easy for them to accidentally listen to songs I don't consider appropriate for their age. Plus they're not necessarily great at remembering the actual title (or even lyrics) of songs.

So I decided to build my own solution. I bought an NFC reader and a stack of ntag 125 cards from Ali express, and repurposed an old computer to play songs from YouTube or YouTube music URLs when the card is left on the reader. My wife added original artwork, but I also bought a cheap thermal sticker printer from Ali express so we could print the actual cover art if we wanted.

To setup a song/album/playlist we simply copy the URL from the YT music app into the NFC tools app, and then tap the tag to our phone.

Here you can see it in action.

If you don't have a spare laptop or raspberry pi, but do have a spare phone with inbuilt NFC reader, you can do something similar by setting the phone to stay always on, and putting it upside down in a lock box like this one, with some foam to keep it pressed to the top of the box. Then whenever you tap the top of the lockbox with the tag it will automatically play the link in the tag.

Altogether I spent less than 60 dollars on this, and have what I think is a great solution for the kids!

item.title: Reddit, AI, and the Era of Data Silos
item.description:
This piece was originally published on my Substack.  I'm around on X / Twitter and LinkedIn.

By most measures, Reddit’s third quarter was a strong one. Revenue grew 53% to $895 million, ahead of expectations. However, the stock fell 29% the next day. The market wasn’t reacting to the Q3 print, but to the fact that Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews were sending fewer people to Reddit, with management indicating that daily users could fall by a low double-digit percentage and guiding to a sharp revenue deceleration in Q4.

That warning isn’t just about Reddit. For two decades, the open web ran on an implicit contract: publishers shared content for free, acquired users through search engines like Google, and monetized through ads. AI is breaking this contract, and the companies that depend on it are being repriced. Reddit, one of the last major social networks that’s still open by default, is in the eye of the storm.

As AI closes off the open web, it’s unclear how businesses like Reddit will monetize going forward, and investors are de-rating them the same way they did SaaS earlier this year. This presents an opening for Reddit, but only if it pulls harder on the two levers it does control: building a product that appeals to the next 100 million users and monetizing its data more aggressively.

In this post, I cover the following:

  • How the open web made money before AI and why that contract is breaking
  • How the shift is already showing up in Reddit’s numbers
  • How Reddit’s move to limit its posts to logged-in users follows in the footsteps of other social networks and signals a broader shift to a closed web
  • What it would take to build Reddit for the next 100 million users
  • The levers that would re-rate Reddit and what to watch for

Let’s dive in.

Why the open web is closing

To level-set the conversation, Ben Thompson’s The Agentic Web and Original Sin is the best primer on how the open web got paid: advertising monetized human attention, and Google was the web’s biggest beneficiary. AI breaks that model in three ways:

  • AI answers: Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode answer the question on the search page, so the click (and the ad impression) never happens
  • Training data: AI labs scrape content to train their models, often without paying for it
  • Agents: when an AI agent browses on a user’s behalf, there’s no human to see the ad

What replaces the old contract is unclear. One option is usage-based access, where AI companies pay each time they crawl a page (Cloudflare’s Pay Per Crawl is an example). Another is a flat, all-you-can-eat licensing deal. Some publishers are even embedding invisible ads meant only for agents. For Reddit, the cost of the old contract breaking is already showing up in its numbers.

Reddit is already losing its Google traffic

Reddit co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman put the blame for the decline in search traffic squarely on Google, with referrals dropping by over a million per week in October 2026.

… Where we're seeing mixed results is total sessions are down because of that decline in search referral traffic…

… on the change from Google, our hypothesis is twofold. The biggest one is AI Overviews or AI Mode … it pushes everyone down the search page. And then on top of that, the experiences themselves are not traffic drivers. And so these things combined with the rollout mean Google has really shifted in their relationship with the rest of the Internet… People still want Reddit. It's just Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to. Given our strategy is to make Reddit a direct destination, this is actually in line with our strategy because Google is teaching people that if you want to come to Reddit, you need to come to Reddit.

… Also, Google is crawling us as hard as ever. So the demand hasn't changed from their point of view either. The reality is AI Mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody as far as I know.

There hasn’t been a large dip in daily active users yet, apart from a drop in US logged-out users, from 30.1 million to 27.3 million QoQ. However, management has guided to a potential sequential low double-digit drop in users in Q4 as a result of Google’s product changes.

The Reddit riposte: building its own data silo

Reddit’s response follows those of other social networks: closing off access to logged-out users, starting with select markets outside the US. Here, management expects the change to cost Reddit reach in exchange for more engaged users. It also makes it harder for AI companies to scrape Reddit’s data, which matters for its data licensing business.

In terms of data licensing, Reddit dropped the ball early. It only started charging for API access in April 2023, months after ChatGPT launched. By then, most of Reddit’s existing corpus had likely already been used for model pretraining, so the value of its data today skews toward new posts (e.g. what users think of the new Camry). Over the past four quarters, Reddit made $166m in “other revenue,” most of which is data licensing. For comparison, Twitter made $572m from data licensing and other revenue in 2021, before the era of frontier AI labs (this revenue includes the MoPub ad exchange). This was ~11% of Twitter’s revenues at the time vs. ~5% of Reddit’s revenues today.

My mental model is that Reddit’s potential customer base falls into two groups: frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic (which Reddit is currently suing), and a long tail of buyers that could include hedge funds and market research firms. As existing deals come up for renewal and new customers sign on, I expect the next set of deals to be much larger.

The crucial question is what the move costs Reddit. On Reddit’s Q3 earnings call, management stated that logged-in and app users drove over 80% of Reddit’s revenue. Based on this, we can back into the ratio of logged-in to logged-out ARPU, which is 5–6x (see chart below).

There are two costs to this move. The first is user growth: logged-out international users drove 85% of Reddit’s DAU growth over the past year, so the logged-in user requirement could hurt the conversion funnel for new logged-in users. The second cost is its potential revenue impact. International users brought in about $193m in Q3 ($2.43 ARPU across 79.6 million users). If logged-in users are worth about 5x logged-out users internationally (the low end of the global range), then international logged-out users drove just under $50m, or roughly 5% of Q3 revenue.

So, Reddit’s logged-in user test is relatively low risk from a revenue perspective. The bigger risk is growth, which is why it’s so crucial for Reddit to focus on its other lever: product design. Specifically, Reddit needs to build an app that can attract and convert more of its 500 million+ weekly visitors, including logged-out users, into engaged daily users.

Building Reddit for the next 100 million users

Going back to the DAU chart earlier in the piece, we see that Reddit’s most valuable users, US logged-in users, have been flat at ~23 million for the past seven quarters, while international logged-in user growth has also been decelerating sharply from ~19% to 11% YoY. The majority of Reddit’s recent growth has come from logged-out international users, who are most at risk from the logged-in requirement.

To sustain healthy growth, Reddit needs to attract more daily users (vs. only increasing ad load). This is extremely important because advertisers can quickly saturate individual subreddits, so a larger daily audience gives Reddit more ad inventory and pricing power. Here, I focus on three product areas that would help Reddit appeal to a broader audience.

The first is content moderation, which has helped drive Reddit’s high gross margins (moderators across subreddits essentially work for free to police the site). However, this is a double-edged sword, because moderation can be inconsistent. Users can get banned or have posts removed for a myriad of reasons (e.g. disagreeing with a moderator’s opinion, obscure subreddit rules, and Reddit’s shadowban mechanism). This reduces the willingness of both new and existing users to engage.

If this persists or gets worse, Reddit might end up like Stack Overflow. While LLMs played a role in Stack Overflow’s decline, user hostility (toward users who both asked and answered questions) was another contributor. Hacker News has plenty of threads on this (e.g. here and here). There’s likely no silver bullet here, but a layered approach might include the following:

  • Appeals: a more robust appeals process beyond appealing to the same moderators that removed a post. This could be an in-house team or moderators from adjacent subreddits
  • AI enforcement: further investment in AI systems that approve or remove posts based on a subreddit’s rules, rather than the biases of specific moderators
  • Community notes: a Twitter Community Notes-like system for highly unpopular or controversial posts

The second is content format. The way users engage with content has changed (e.g. shorter attention spans, more passive consumption). Other platforms have already adapted. To compete against TikTok, YouTube introduced Shorts, and Instagram added Reels. Reddit, in contrast, is still text-heavy (which is part of its appeal!), so it needs to iterate on how it can thoughtfully incorporate additional modalities.

To that end, I’ve been studying Chinese social app RedNote (小红书). Originally a PDF shopping guide, RedNote has gone through several product evolutions. Today, its recommendation feed supports multiple modalities, including text, images, short-form video, and live streaming. Users engage by clicking into a specific post. The interesting product experience is that when they click into a video or live stream, scrolling down triggers a TikTok-like experience. This gives users multiple “user journeys.” The challenge for Reddit is building a seamless experience, especially for its mobile app, that allows users to intuitively trigger non-text product experiences while preserving its core value prop.

The third recommendation is more nebulous. It’s less about a specific product and more about how quickly Reddit ships and follows shifts in user behavior. To be fair, Reddit is adding product enhancements at a good cadence (AI translations for international users, AI search, and recently Reddit Reviews). But these efforts haven’t resulted in a reacceleration in user growth yet. As AI tools answer more questions directly and the open web becomes more siloed, more platforms will be walled gardens. So, after Reddit removes unfettered access to its data, it can either be a data source for general platforms like ChatGPT or Google, or it can be a destination itself. For example, if a user is searching for an espresso machine, what if instead of asking ChatGPT, which does a web search, Reddit becomes the default destination? This gives Reddit another way to capture ad dollars and allows it to win search queries vs. general-purpose platforms.

Reddit should also be testing longer-term, strategic bets. For example, one trend is that more conversations are moving from public town squares like Reddit and X into private chats on Discord, WhatsApp, and Telegram. The exact product surface here is unclear. It could be a more full-featured chat product within Reddit, or a separate app. Regardless, these are the kinds of experiments Reddit should start running now.

Reddit is moving in the right direction but needs to be far more aggressive

Closing off access to logged-out users and pushing for larger data licensing deals are the right moves as the web becomes more siloed. Furthermore, there’s enough headroom in both of Reddit’s levers to sustain high growth for the next few years. On the user side, Reddit already has 500 million+ weekly visitors, so product improvements and marketing can drive growth by converting more of them into daily users. On the data side, licensing is still only ~5% of revenue, so there’s headroom there as well.

The market isn’t giving Reddit much credit for that today. Reddit trades at ~11x forward earnings vs. ~19x for Meta, even though Reddit guided to ~40% revenue growth next quarter vs. ~25% for Meta (Meta is growing on a much larger revenue base, however). On a growth-adjusted basis, Reddit’s PEG of 0.35 is the same as Pinterest’s and roughly a third of Meta’s (0.97).

If the following signals turn positive, the current multiple leaves a lot of room for a re-rating:

  • Users: whether daily users fall as much as management warned when Reddit reports Q4 in February, and whether US users stabilize
  • Product velocity: how quickly Reddit fixes well-known problems (e.g. moderation) and introduces new features
  • Licensing: the size of the next round of data deals for both renewals and new customers

Similar to SaaS companies earlier this year, content businesses are now facing their own crucible moment. But there’s still significant fog of war around how social media platforms will evolve in the age of AI. This is an opening for Reddit if it moves much more aggressively. And as Huffman put it, “Google is teaching people that if you want to come to Reddit, you need to come to Reddit.” Reddit needs to give those users a reason to stay.

Disclosure: I may hold positions in the companies discussed in this piece. Nothing here is investment advice.

item.title: Conscious and Unconscious Processsing
item.description:
[LW Meta: this post is essentially (a) brief intro to section 3 of the 'thermontology' sequence/website (b) a meta-summary of Kaj's post Book Summary: Consciousness and the Brain ]

3.0 Now let's talk about higher-level things than physics!

3.0.1 I'm going to write about a seemingly random collection of things in the biological and social worlds, connected by three themes:

  • 3.0.1.1 Amplification. Things which amplify information, copying something small and local to a larger scale. Biological reproduction, networks in the brain, and interpersonal attention are some examples.
  • 3.0.1.2 History. Amplification events are conditioned on past events, producing a chain. This is history; it enables iterative optimization. As history progresses, equilibrium is approached: it becomes harder and harder for a localized change to propagate to global scale.
  • 3.0.1.3 Ambiguity. Things can be interpreted in many ways. A teacup can be used for drinking, but it also might strike you as artistic inspiration, or remind you of days gone by. People, organisms, ideas have an intrinsic dependence on the context in which they arise and exist.

3.0.2 As you might guess, I ultimately want to analogize these things to the phenomena in physics from the last section. Just to clear up any confusion, I'm not claiming that social networks use quantum entanglement to function or something like that. It's more of a structural analogy. I'll get more into this in section 4.

3.1 Amplification in the Brain

3.1.0.1 What is consciousness and how does it relate to the brain? This question has baffled philosophers for centuries. Tabling the philosophical questions about what consciousness even is, though, neuroscience has actually made a lot of progress on a more well-defined question: what's the difference between the processing in the brain of which people are aware, and that which they are not aware of?

3.1.0.2 The material in this section is shamelessly stolen from Kaj Sotala's excellent post Book Summary: Consciousness and the Brain. The rest of his Multiagent Models of Mind sequence is excellent too.

3.1.1 Conscious and Unconscious Processing

3.1.1.1 It's clear that people aren't conscious of almost all of the processing that's going on in their brain. The brain contains ~10^11 neurons and ~10^15 synapses. Each neuron fires about once per second. Obviously we aren't aware of almost any of this. On the other hand, we do have awareness of some things, such as the content of our visual fields.

3.1.1.2 Wait, how do we even define aware? Let's say that people are consciously aware of things that they can verbally report.

3.1.1.3 So what determines the difference between things people are aware of and things they aren't? Neuroscientists have carried out a series of ingenious experiments to determine the boundary between these things.

3.1.1.4 The basic idea is as follows. If you very rapidly turn certain stimuli on and then off, people aren't able to notice that they were there at all. However, you can determine that some part of their brain processed the stimulus, because their performance on tasks related to the stimulus improves.

3.1.1.5 One basic paradigm in these experiments is visual masking. A subject is told to look at a screen on which various geometric shapes are shown[1]. For a very brief interval, the shapes are replaced with some sort of meaningful stimulus such as the word "radio". By controlling the interval for which the stimulus is shown, researchers can control how often subjects report seeing it. If the word is shown for 40ms, nobody sees it; at 50ms, about half can see it.

3.1.1.6 Priming experiments show that the subject's brain has nevertheless processed the word, even if they aren't consciously aware of it. The idea is to give subjects a task to complete about 1 second after the word is shown. For instance, after the word "radio" is flashed, subjects might be shown the word "house" and asked to classify it as either a living thing or an object. If the word the subjects are shown is the same as the flashed "priming" word, they are quicker to classify it.

3.1.1.7 Unconscious processing goes beyond mere visual similarity. For instance, the uppercase "RADIO" helps to speed up processing lowercase "radio", although they have very different visual appearances. And contrarily, "ANGER" does not speed up "RANGE", although they have the same letters, suggesting that the meaning of the words is important for the unconscious processing. Quite complex processing can happen without awareness: for instance, chess masters shown a chess position can more quickly classify the position as a check if they are primed with the same position.

3.1.1.8 Besides speeding up conscious decisions, unconscious information can also be used to guide decisions directly, and for learning. In one experiment subjects were tasked with pressing or not pressing a button after being shown a signal (the signal giving no information about which choice was correct). Choosing correctly earned them money. The signals were preceded by briefly-flashed masked shapes which indicated whether pressing or not pressing was the correct response. Although the shapes were shown too briefly to register in consciousness, subjects learned to choose correctly at a better-than-chance rate.

  • 3.1.1.8.1 Kaj's post has many more examples demonstrating unconscious processing in masking experiments.

3.1.1.9 So unconscious processing can do a lot. Besides verbal report, what does conscious processing add?

  • 3.1.1.9.1 Memory. Things which reach consciousness can be recalled later when needed. Memory also enables learning relationships between things which are separated by more than a few seconds.
  • 3.1.1.9.2 Sequential chained operations. Consciousness enables chaining together cognitive operations sequentially. In experiments testing people's ability to do arithmetic unconsciously, it was found that one-step operations such as adding 2 to a single-digit number, or determining if a digit was less than 5, could be done successfully about half the time even if subjects were not conscious of seeing the digit. However, multi-step operations such as adding 2 to a number then determining if it was smaller than 5, were performed no better than chance unconsciously.
  • 3.1.1.9.3 Conscious decisions are usually far more accurate and reliable than unconscious ones, even if the latter are better than chance.

3.1.1.10 One other set of experiments people ran concerned the rivalrous nature of consciousness; in other words, consciousness can only strongly focus on one thing at a time. People are shown a series of digits into which 2 letters are inserted. They're told to remember the letters; if the letters are shown too quickly after each other, they may not even notice that the second letter was present. Focusing on the first letter prevents the second from entering consciousness.

  • 3.1.1.10.1 This famous video, which tasks viewers with counting the number of times a baseball was passed, is another good example.

3.1.1.11 So that's a brief overview of some experimental evidence we have regarding conscious and unconscious processing. Given this, what can we say about how they are implemented in the brain?

3.1.2 The Global Neuronal Workspace

3.1.2.1 People have run variants of the masking experiments above where they (a) hook up the subjects to an apparatus for measuring brain activity, such as an MRI, EEG, or MEG, and (b) intentionally vary the length of the stimuli presented so that some of the stimuli reach consciousness. Then researchers try to identify differences in brain activity between conscious and unconscious perception.

3.1.2.2 The basic result people have found is that consciousness of a stimulus happens when the neural signal associated with the stimulus exceeds a threshold and is amplified and spreads to distant regions of the brain, whereas unconscious stimuli's signals remain localized to a particular part of the brain and fade away.

3.1.2.3 How does this amplification take place? There are various long-range interconnections between different regions of the cortex. These interconnections feed back on each other, and when a given signal becomes strong enough it can kick off a self-reinforcing loop that eventually synchronizes a large part of the brain on processing the given signal.

3.1.2.4 This is called the "global neuronal workspace". Aside from the cortex, the GNW also connects to the basal ganglia, thalamus, hippocampus, and other parts of the brain. The GNW theory of consciousness posits that the contents of consciousness are precisely the things that the GNW is processing in a given moment.

3.1.2.5 The GNW explains various features of consciousness:

  • 3.1.2.5.1 Consciousness is binary: you either see a signal or you don't. This is because of the threshold effect: either a signal is strong enough to set off a cascade in the GNW, or it isn't.
  • 3.1.2.5.2 Consciousness is rivalrous. If a given stimulus has already begun propagating in the GNW, this makes it more difficult for a new signal to recruit neurons to amplify it.
  • 3.1.2.5.3 Consciousness enables memory and verbal report, by connecting incoming stimuli to parts of the brain responsible for speech (parts of the cortex) and long-term memory (the hippocampus).

3.1.2.6 So what's the biological function of consciousness? There are probably a few. Here are some speculations.

  • 3.1.2.6.1 The brain is highly parallel because parallelism is more energy-efficient and easier to scale. However, parallelism has certain drawbacks.
  • 3.1.2.6.2 Firstly, different brain regions need to talk to each other, to exchange information. The GNW facilitates this, although there are other pathways in the brain that do as well.
  • 3.1.2.6.3 For the purposes of planning and motor output, the brain needs to decide on a single, coherent plan. Thus there needs to be some mechanism for getting regions of the brain to agree and sync up on the current global plan. The winner-takes-all dynamics of the GNW can do this.
  • 3.1.2.6.4 When planning and acting, you need to prioritize, decide what to do next. Sometimes this might take the form of needing to suddenly switch your attention to something important, e.g. responding to a sudden loud noise behind you in the woods at night. But there's also a constant need to decide e.g. what step of a plan to carry out next, what word to use next when writing, where to look when searching for something. The GNW helps with this by implementing a sort of "attentional Darwinism" where a vast number of hypotheses can be implicitly searched over, with the winning ideas gaining support and being promoted to the GNW.
  1. ^

    The purpose of the shapes is to prevent subjects from noticing a small flicker when the word appears, as might happen if the screen was black.
