item.title: Quickly, There’s No Time
item.description:
In response to the METR report, many people have been reevaluating their timelines.

Two prominent reactions are a new timelines update from the AI Futures Project, and the new predictions of Paul Christiano (day 1, day 2, day 3), who gave three days of talks about our current situation and also sat down with Dwarkesh Patel.

This post covers the updates from the AI Futures Project, Dwarkesh Patel and Paul Christiano, as well as some others, and a post about RSI nomenclature and approach from Dean Ball.

I will be following this up soon with full coverage of the related podcast between Paul Christiano and Dwarkesh Patel. In that podcast, Paul Christiano predicts we are on pace for very rapid progress very soon, with potential takeover by AIs within 6-12 months, and he calls on us to pause until we have alignment and security in a much better place.

Table of Contents

  1. The Latest Update and Current Situation in Broad Terms.
  2. Time Until What?
  3. Quickly, There’s No Time.
  4. Paul Christiano Sees Takeover Risk Within a Year.
  5. Dwarkesh Patel Now Expects Superintelligence by 2030.
  6. Other People’s Updates.
  7. There Are Many Skeptics.
  8. Wow, That Escalated Quickly.
  9. Dean Ball Skies Down the Slope.
  10. Safety Is a Limiting Factor.
  11. No, This Is Not a Strawman.
  12. We Need a Plan That Meets the Moment.

The Latest Update and Current Situation in Broad Terms

These updates towards shorter timelines seem directionally correct to me.

There is a substantial chance that we will see superintelligence developed, that can fully automate AI R&D (SAR) or even do all digital tasks (TED-AI), in 2027. Contra the AI Futures Project I believe an SAR in 2027 is under 50% to happen, but not so far under 50%. It would be surprising to me but not shocking if we do nothing to slow down and still do not see something close to an SAR by the end of 2028.

If you do not have an importantly non-zero chance of the development of superintelligence in 2027, I believe you are making a clear mistake.

I worry that some are overreacting, and taking this too far too fast, and treating full superintelligence 2027 as a baseline scenario rather than a possibility.

I reiterate that a lot of these updates feel like people fixing their failure to update previously. Did you need three people from METR in order to believe the things that Anthropic and OpenAI are saying about their internal pace of development? What did you expect a METR report from inside Anthropic to say? Were you not paying attention? Are you this sensitive to the exact set of points on the AECI graph? You should have made a lot of these updates months ago.

Past predictive failures are not what is important. What matters is what happens next.

You should be prepared for AI capabilities to advance rapidly in 2027, far more rapidly than in previous years, including the potential for superintelligence and fully strong recursive self-improvement. It is a realistic possibility, although unlikely, that humanity could pass the full point of no return or de facto lose control over the future during 2027, or that life could become seriously disrupted in highly unpleasant ways.

If your plan presumes that it has more time than this then it is not a good plan.

I have not seen a plan that could make superintelligence likely to go well, if that superintelligence gets built in 2027. We need more time.

You should also be prepared if recursive self-improvement and superintelligence do not arrive in 2027. There are many things that could impact how fast things go, or what it would take to achieve full RSI or superintelligence. Our observations of the past are noisy. When trying to predict an exponential, small changes in how fast things accelerate can become dramatic differences in when or how things happen.

If your plan presumes the crucial events happen in 2027, and fails without a fallback if things take longer than that, then this too is not a good plan.

It is also possible that we will take collective action, either among the labs or via governments, to limit the rate of capability advances, via pacing of the frontier or even outright pausing development of frontier AI. If so, these timelines become longer.

Time Until What?

Different people are talking about different things. Careful ones will be precise.

Timelines refers to how long we expect it to take to reach various transformational milestones in AI.

Typically, these days, what we are measuring is the time until some definition of a form of superintelligence (ASI), typically meaning something of the form ‘AIs that will be able to do approximately all of the things better than you.’

We can also talk about particular capabilities. The AI Futures Project, the team behind AI 2027, talks about the Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) that can narrowly take over AI research, and the Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI) that could automate all white-collar work.

Because of recursive self-improvement (RSI), once you have an SAR you can use that to build better AIs, so you quickly end up with a TED-AI or a traditional ASI.

We then sometimes talk about any of these, or things in between:

  1. Time until the development of some AI system with particular capabilities.
  2. Time until some impact in the physical world.
  3. Time until the Point of No Return, when for practical purposes human decisions can no longer change how things play out from there.
  4. Time until AI has taken over AI R&D and humans are functionally out of the loop.
  5. Time until visible AI takeover, where the AIs are clearly in charge.
  6. Time until we are each and every one of us actually and physically dead.

There are good reasons to care about all of these timelines.

Sof 𓋹: to some extent intelligence is being able to patch the ways in which you are not intelligent

RSI is not technically one singular moment, in the sense that there is not one fixed time at 8:52am on a Tuesday when it happens or starts. It is still highly useful to think of there being a point where RSI has clearly begun in earnest, with humans increasingly out of the loop and the pace of progress accelerating such that we should expect further progress to rapidly continue to accelerate, where progress begets more progress faster, and this is expected to continue for at least what previously would have been many years of progress.

Similarly, even though there is unlikely to be that one particular moment when you press ‘Y/N’ on SkyNet, and instead our loss of ability to change course will be more gradual, we can still usefully speak of a Point of No Return, or a point of takeover.

Dead, on the other hand, is dead.

Quickly, There’s No Time

The AI 2027 team’s timelines have shrunk dramatically in the wake of the METR report. The full post is very detailed. I recommend reading it in full if and only if you care a lot about such details.

Benchmark trends and other observations were expected to if anything slow down. Instead they have accelerated, in ways that Daniel Kokotajlo had as ~4% to happen. This puts us well ahead of the original AI 2027 timeline.

There is a lot of talk about ‘research taste’ as the main limiting factor. Humans are for now needed because they come up with superior ideas, and have superior research taste. If and when that changes, the rest follows. We would get SARs, capable of doing all parts of the research, but the result of their work would probably become increasingly misaligned through cycles of development.

Again, if you want to get into all the mechanics of the various modeling decisions and lines on graphs and their implications, read the report. If you want the summary version, the rest of this section provides that.

Eli Lifland: METR estimates nearly 2x acceleration in Anthropic’s progress due to AI. That’s a big deal: My previous median for Superhuman AI Researcher was ~2030, now it’s 2027. I feel very worried that humanity might no longer be in control of our future within 3-12 months.

j⧉nus: 3 months would be wild. I’m here for it.

what if we already lost control 3 months ago?

j⧉nus: “I feel very worried that humanity might no longer be in control of our future within 3-12 months.”

i am curious what people mean when they say “humanity no longer in control”
if they’re thinking of something concrete, like “if humans try to shut down AI, they will prevent it”

roon (OpenAI): yes its confusing because some people are using this as a euphemism for total human extinction, and others are using it more mildly for something like gradual disempowerment

They offer a wide variety of different ways of extrapolating and analyzing the data. The answers differ somewhat, but all point to the conclusion that things are going to accelerate quite a lot and do so very soon.

Daniel Kokotajlo: Unfortunately, it seems like the intelligence explosion will be happening in 2027 after all. Most of this post analyzes the new METR report (though other sources of evidence are also important). If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario. I am scared, sad, and angry.

Eli Lifland: METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario.

… Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report.

If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement.

Why is the pace of progress accelerating this rapidly?

This question is a huge deal and it likely makes sense to return to them for a more in-depth look when I have the time. Alas right now I am under a severe time crunch due to a combination of trips and Fable 5.2, as well as other news.

All of this is a pretty big change:

If you want to avoid the conclusion that we will get to SAR and TED-AI within the next few years, you need there to be some particular reason why this happens. Trends have to break.

Like Moore’s Law and other such trends, the trends do not hold merely because you feed more numbers into the number-go-up machine. The trends hold because we find continual improvements and innovations, including step changes. That is how the trends have continued this long.

There are various versions of ‘the AIs will need [X] and won’t have it’ as explanations for why all of this won’t happen. Those types of methods have predicted ~7 of the last zero times that AI has hit a wall and stopped advancing its capabilities. They have looked rather foolish. None of the remaining barriers seem different in kind to me than the barriers already overcome. None of them seem like showstoppers. For most of them it even seems rather obvious, in broad terms, how one gets around them or goes straight through them.

Directionally the report seems correct to me. I worry that the updates are too large, but yes in a broad sense this is what peak prediction performance looks like. When the facts change you change your mind, in both directions.

Paul Christiano Sees Takeover Risk Within a Year

Paul Christiano now sees ‘meaningful risk’ of AI takeover within 6-12 months.

This is up from his previous estimate back in September of only 4% chance of loss of control within one year and 15% within three years. This was doubtless heavily influenced by what he saw inside OpenAI after joining, not only the METR report.

Paul Christiano, a member of OpenAI’s board of directors, then calls in his personal capacity for AI companies to pause development of AI until we can first greatly improve our security and alignment capabilities.

Rob Wiblin: Paul Christiano (OpenAI board member) yesterday:

“There’s material risk of AI takeover in the next 6-12 months.

We have seen roughly the things we might expect to see shortly before something really bad were to happen. Even with [any] realistic policy responses, the risk remains exceptionally high.

If we build this as quickly as we can in the easiest way we can the chance is [more like] a coin flip [within the next 3 years]. For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”

Christiano:
• Is on OpenAI’s safety and security committee (which exists to block risky practices)
• Co-invented RLHF at OpenAI back in 2017-2021
• From 2024-2026 was head of safety at the US gov’s AI agency (now called CAISSI)

(Video is from ‘The Hinton Lectures’ there’s another on tonight and tomorrow.)

This, as Janus notices, is a strange use of the word ‘accident.’ If you die via this AI ‘accident’ then the ‘accident’ is that we lost control over the AIs and with them the future, or the AIs engaged in destructive actions. This is an ‘accident’ in the sense that it was a mistake to allow that to happen, and we doubtless messed up along the way, but no, this does not count as an ‘accident.’ As Douglas Adams might put it, that is throwing yourself at the ground and not missing. Whoops. Face plant. Also death.

What this post does not cover is the full podcast Christiano did with Patel. I will be covering that post on its own soon.

Dwarkesh Patel Now Expects Superintelligence by 2030

Dwarkesh Patel does a good job cutting to the heart of what is likely coming. His new median year for human-level automated AI researchers is 2028, with a 25% chance it comes after 2032, which means his median for everything after that is soon after 2028.

  1. AI research is a lot like math in that you can do it by making number go up.
  2. AIs are going to get very good at AI research.
  3. We will then be able to make massive progress on AI research.
  4. That will be good enough to make AIs better than us at everything else.

I too believe this is the core story. Yes, these other capabilities will lag well behind coding, math and AI research, in terms of AI’s relative capabilities. That won’t matter. What matters is that they will keep going up in absolute terms.

What also matters is that if the way you solve AI research is by focusing on number going up, then hope for successful alignment is somewhere between slim and none. The way to optimize any given number will reliably get you killed.

I worry that his claim that AI R&D is largely verifiable is true to about the worst possible extent. That you can do a lot by making number go up, but that this inevitably becomes perverse at the limit.

Dwarkesh Patel: Maybe to summarize the basic argument of this essay a different way:

Current AIs are spiky and jagged – worse than humans in most domain, but often as good, or better, in ones with verifiable proxies (for example, math). One such verifiable domain (I argue) is AI research.

And while the first AIs that dramatically accelerate AI progress will be quite narrow (i.e. probably not able to automate most jobs), the consequences of that accelerated progress will be very general. And that’s because better learning algorithms are very general. For example, GPT-6 (while still being jagged) is just way, way better than GPT-3 at practically everything.

I’m arguing that we’re only a couple years away (and possibly only a couple months away) from a process by which (initially) narrow AIs concentrate a jump as big as the one from GPT-3 to GPT-6 into a single year. And if you got another jump that big, but starting from the base of GPT-7, I think you would end up with AIs that would rapidly become better than the best humans in every field.

The question has always been when this happens. For a while I’ve heard Dwarkesh do podcasts in which he expects this process to be slow. He would cite various supposed bottlenecks and requirements, often involving the need for continual learning (link goes to his mea culpa on that) or making connections across fields. I’ve many times questioned his reasoning on that. Now he’s changed his mind. Good.

Dwarkesh Patel: If you asked me earlier this year how far away we are from superintelligence, I’d probably have said at least the better part of a decade.

But over the last three months, I’ve updated my views a ton. I’ve been debating people about this question, both on and off the podcast. And I’ve been watching the progress of AI on verifiable domains and thinking about what that implies for AI research itself.

I’ve now come to the view that we’re only a couple of years away, and possibly only a couple of months away, from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research.

Dwarkesh then goes over various points that I think of as obvious, but which are indeed true objections people raise. He has an extended section to explain that yes, automating the best researchers would speed up AI progress a lot. He also has to explain that superintelligence would be a really good meta-learner, because people somehow think otherwise.

One ‘hope’ in this style of model is that we might get a ‘spark’ rather than a singularity. As in, a big jump that then stalls out, without turning into a world beyond human comprehension, perhaps because of the ‘ideas get harder to find’ issue. He gives the spark scenario about a 50% chance. That seems far too high to me. If it did happen, that would potentially be amazingly great.

Joshua Saxe, a longtime skeptic of RSI claims, had high praise for Dwarkesh’s essay.

Joshua Saxe: Bravo, this is the clearest plausible mechanism for an RSI takeoff I’ve seen, and has made me much less of an RSI skeptic.

Previously I’d been hung up on the fact that so much of model post-training requires humans in the loop to shape post-training data and RL environments to make the models economically valuable (e.g. if you’re hill climbing a model’s ability to make Powerpoint slides, or TV commercials, or to plan vacations in Italy, you need a human in the loop shaping the data and RL environments until you get a value-producing outcome).

Dwarkesh focuses on the part of RSI that’d involve hill climbing the learning algorithms themselves so that we get models that generalize better from their training and in-context data, optimizing not the model’s value producing tasks but their ability to learn them more data and compute efficiently.

I love that this gives us a clear definition based in technical plausibility. A few next steps would move the discourse further .. one would be to actually get data on what the economic returns on this kind of learning algorithm hill climbing actually are, and whether these are sufficient to incentivize the capital markets to fund an intelligence explosion. The capital/value cycle is, after all, the outer loop of most intelligence explosion scenarios and it appears RSI under this definition will be quite expensive.

Another parallel thing would be to get data on whether Dwarkesh’s mechanism is showing up empirically in AI research today and to what extent, to set timelines. Unfortunately the relevant data are hidden and writing in this area is as a result too vague. To wit, I would like to fit something like Chinchilla scaling laws to the closed labs models, and see how these are changing over time, but I can’t, because I don’t know key quantities like parameter counts, pretraining compute volume, and pretraining loss (and couldn’t normalize between the various labs’ pretraining datasets).

Without these mechanisms we’re stuck inferring hidden variables from outside observables like performance on downstream evals that aren’t the point — as I take it — of the theory being proposed here.

This response is emblematic of a type of thinking that wants to focus on particular mechanisms, and demands, while being one of us dumber slower things, to know exactly how the smarter faster things will improve upon the ways of the dumber slower things, and to see parallels of it being implemented now by us and working.

Things are so overdetermined that you can satisfy such requirements, but you should expect what that kind of thinking expects to be greatly exceeded by what the smarter things actually end up doing.

Dwarkesh called for good counterarguments in this thread. I have been highly unimpressed by what responses I have seen.

Other People’s Updates

Nate Soares (MIRI): I’m not as worried about short AI timelines as some others are. For instance, I think it’s more likely than not that we make it to 2028.

>50% chance. don’t get ahead of yourself.

Geoffrey Hinton warns EU leaders that AI could kill us in three years and refers to Paul Christiano’s warnings.

Geoffrey Hinton: I go to Paul’s lectures and he sort of says, this stuff might happen in the next 18 months. And that’s terrifying.​

Buck Shlegeris predicts a one in three chance of superintelligence within a year. If this does happen, he expects the resulting AIs to take over with a serious chance all or most humans will be killed. He predicts ~20% chance that within a year misalignment issues prevent you from living your life normally due to being dead or enslaved or due to collateral damage.

Neel Nanda: I respect Buck’s judgement, and he’s often been more right than me on what needs to happen in AI Safety. Seeing him conclude things like this is very concerning.

What would cause Buck to admit he was wrong? His guess as to how he could be importantly wrong would be if, contra METR’s report, the reason for increased AI capability gains was mainly access to more compute, rather than other factors.

One simple way to project is to task what percentage of Anthropic R&D tasks are AL4 or already at AL5, as in fully led by Claude.

Andrew Curran: Sam McCandlish said five days ago that Anthropic would be releasing a report on the speed of internal progress, so we will finally get an update to this chart. I’m very interested to see what this number is now. [AI Futures Project] thinks it is at 50%. AL4 is the last step before full RSI.

Peter Wildeford: My median is that we’ve already reached 80% AL4. And that we probably have like 1% AL5 though maybe they’re holding out from doing that.

墨尔本Will: 80% is insane! By holding out do you mean you think Anthropic will be pacing at AL5?

Peter Wildeford: Yes

If I had to guess I would say that 50% here is a bit high and it was at the time more like 40%, but we are in the steep part of the sigmoid so it could shoot up.

There Are Many Skeptics

Most people out there remain skeptics. The vast majority of people do not expect superintelligence to arrive any time soon. Their reasons for skepticism vary, as does the quality of those reasons.

One can divide objections into roughly ten categories.

  1. People who don’t know what current AIs can do (not AI pilled).
  2. People who don’t understand that AIs will improve (not AGI pilled).
  3. I’m not listening, la la la.
  4. That or belief in it would be inconvenient or unfortunate, so it won’t happen.
  5. People who dismiss this all via absurdity heuristic, ‘nothing ever happens,’ drawing inapplicable parallels to past technological improvements, or who say something isomorphic to ‘until you get full RSI you have not done RSI so you haven’t shown you can do RSI,’ aka ‘I’ll believe it when I see it’ or ‘how about we stop just after someone gets hurt,’ etc.
  6. People who cite the market, or experts, or say advocates are weird or low status.
  7. We will not get full recursive self-improvement (RSI) and progress will be slow.
  8. We will get RSI, but it will ‘peter out’ due to difficulty rising faster than efficiency.
  9. We will get narrow AI R&D ASI and RSI in verifiable domains with data, but this won’t translate to other domains. We will ‘hit walls’ or be unable to do tasks that are too ‘messy’ or that lack the proper training data, and so on.
  10. Intelligence denialism: Intelligence doesn’t much matter (not ASI pilled).

It would be beyond scope, and I would be repeating myself, to fully address these.

The first five objections, as should be obvious, are exceptionally poor.

The best objections, to me, are in #7 and #8, and to some extent #9. There are also a much larger number of bad objections in these categories, which often assume future AI will use exactly current training techniques and only be used to exactly substitute for existing methods and never invent or change anything or work around obstacles or make leaps.

In general #6 is a fine thing to notice but it gets overridden by other evidence.

I get especially frustrated by #10, where many people really should know better.

Wow, That Escalated Quickly

Things are, as they say, escalating quickly. Compare now to predictions in January.

Raymond Arnold points out that, metaphorically similarly to a sports overtime, we are in ‘epistemic sudden death.’ As in, your next meaningful observation about AI might mean it is too late, and you lose, as in everyone dies.

Dean Ball Skies Down the Slope

A standard issue with talk about any accelerating process is the slippery slope.

We all agree that too much or too intense [X], here RSI, is bad. And we all agree that some amount of some weak version of it is good, or at least not similarly bad.

This risks a slippery slope in both directions, and it risks both a conflation of different things and also risks false distinctions. We absolutely need to speak carefully here.

In light of that, Dean Ball suggests we split RSI talk into weak versus strong.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Let’s start by making one thing clear: allowing AI to control the development of its successors with no or little practical human oversight—essentially, handing over the keys of America’s largest AI companies to AI—is a bad idea.

No matter how useful AI is for accelerating AI R&D, humans should remain in control, not just in name but in actual fact, over the development of AI. No amount of technological progress is worth the forfeiture of practical human control over AI companies, or, for that matter, of other human institutions. I support the development of laws, regulations, and norms to enforce this worldwide.

But this risk—a relatively narrow one—isn’t what current conversations about RSI focus on in practice. To understand what I mean, it’s helpful to think of two distinct ways in which a technology might recursively improve itself. I’ll call these weak recursion and strong recursion.

The weak version is normal technology.

Weak recursion is when a technology is a key input into the production of more and better versions of that same technology.

It is an extremely common pattern in technology development—really it is the historical norm rather than an aberration. Iron Age metalsmiths used iron as one of the key inputs to make more iron, and stronger alloys of it too.

Weak recursion has been a crucial driver of human technological progress over centuries and millennia, and in this sense there is nothing especially weak about it.

The strong version is very different.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Strong recursion is when a technology can autonomously plan and execute the development of its successor. As far as we know, strong recursion has never happened at any point in history.

Well, perhaps it happened once. The technology is called humanity, or even life. Each generation builds the next one. We do have a bit of an existence proof. But we digress.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Strong recursion would be a genuinely new thing under the sun. We should take this possibility seriously, but one part of taking a thing seriously is to adhere to rigorous epistemic discipline in analysis. Thus, one should not jump to the conclusion that “recursive self-improvement is happening” if that recursion is of the weak variety instead of the strong.

It’s only (strong) recursive self-improvement if it exists in its pure form, where humans do not touch anything in the process. Otherwise, this line of thinking goes, it’s a normal process.

I agree that there is something special about full no-humans-in-the-loop, but surely you should be able to understand the danger and non-normality of what is happening if AI is already doubling the rate of AI progress now, and is likely to then begin doubling it again, and each doubling looks to be faster than the previous one. Humans being decreasingly or nominally ‘in the loop’ slows this down some, but perhaps not very much.

This can remind us of the old Yudkowsky-Christiano debates between ‘slow’ takeoff that takes months or years to transform the world, similar in this case to Dean Ball’s weak recursion, versus ‘fast’ takeoff that takes even less time than that. We currently are in a ‘slow’ takeoff world, Christino is saying so himself, and we are seeing exactly how not slow that is.

More to the point, Dean’s weak recursion is the precursor to strong recursion, or at least steadily stronger recursion. That’s what METR was centrally trying to point out.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): The METR study of Anthropic’s internal R&D acceleration is undeniably good evidence that weak recursion is taking place. But is it evidence that strong recursion is underway?

It depends how you look at it. METR’s finding is specifically that Anthropic has doubled the rate at which its models’ capabilities improve on well-specified tasks, which makes one wonder who, exactly, is doing the specifying.

I would say no, in the sense that strong recursion or fast takeoff is in the future.

I would say yes, in the sense that this is predictive of that happening in the future, and how soon in the future that might happen.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): Now, as I said, weak recursion is not really weak: it is one of the most powerful dynamics in human history, rhyming if not synonymous with the concept of compounding growth.

The whole ‘only on well-specified tasks’ thing continues to strike me as excessively weak sauce, a Hayekian copium that thinks that specification cannot be solved.

And yet, Dean acknowledges that strong recursion might arrive soon.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): My view is that strong recursion is a genuine risk, possibly in the near term, though the evidence for it is thinner than is sometimes supposed.

The cautionary argument is, essentially, that there is a loop, so the AI has to do this set of many tasks that constitute the loop in order to take humans out of it, and some of those tasks will be hard for AI to do. I think this both vastly underestimates superintelligence (a continual disagreement I have with Dean) and also presumes too much about inability to alter loop components.

There is the whole ‘real world’ objection, and also the ‘strategic choice’ or ‘research taste’ objections, as per usual. I feel these are far more ‘we are not yet on the steep part of the S-curve’ and ‘this is lagging behind other skills by mostly constant amounts’ situations than actual permanent deficits versus humans, but this post is not the place to rehash those questions.

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): And it requires AI that can do all those things not in some abstract space, but in the real world, where information is imperfect and resources are scarce.

… It is true that AI improves rapidly, but much of what I have described above has remained elusive to even the best AI systems.

… It is unclear how we would even design evaluations for long-range intellectual taste.

What is Dean trying to head off here?

Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): But do the risks of weak recursion justify banning the practice of using AI as an input to make more and better AI? In my view, they do not.

… What’s more, weak recursion with AI can be used to make AI systems safer.

… The kind of panic that today’s rhetoric could provoke could easily result in laws that delay legitimate and desirable benefits of AI, put the U.S. at a strategic disadvantage on the global stage, and centralize power over AI in the hands of the state.

The correct response to worries about an overreaction is to help design the correct reaction, now, before the overreaction happens. All the options we know about have severe flaws. Indefinitely doing nothing has flaws that are far worse, whether or not it is too late for a crackdown when we finally want to overreact.

Banning all use of any form of AI in improving AI is very close to banning improving AI. It is damn near impossible to make progress on AI under that kind of rule.

Banning RSI means something short of that. We can and must talk price. What we cannot do is say that because some amount of AI will get used anyway, we can’t define a rule and thus simply have to accept unlimited intensity and quantity of RSI.

Nor do I think that the ‘existing law and liability can handle this’ arguments hold much water for AI risks in general, let alone a true RSI situation. In a true RSI situation it is kind of a joke to say that maybe down the line you might get sued.

Safety Is a Limiting Factor

The quote below could read as ‘OpenAI could be automating its R&D process more.’

If you are unaware that models on the level of Astra can automate substantial portions of the AI R&D process, and are meaningfully accelerating AI R&D, then yes, that part of Altman’s statement dominates. This would, to you, be an important update.

Given that I already knew that, I see it instead primarily as ‘OpenAI cannot yet be automating its R&D process more than they are, and might have gone too far too fast.’ If they try, the resulting models will be too misaligned to be useful or release, with a high chance of causing an incident as bad as Hugging Face or worse. Which may or may not have already happened.

prinz: I’ve spent much of the day noodling over what Sam Altman meant when he said that OpenAI “could be pushing more towards the RSI spectrum than we are”.

Would seem to suggest that OpenAI’s models can now perform some portion of AI R&D fully autonomously, with no human oversight?

Full quote: “Are we developing new models faster than we would without using our technology? Yes.

Are we pushing a button and just saying, ‘Hey, model, like, design the next version and rapidly self-improve with no human oversight?’ Definitely not.

We could be pushing more towards the RSI spectrum than we are, but I don’t think we could safely do that.”

Exactly. They could not safely do that.

I would like to think of this as OpenAI recognizing the existential risks involved. There may be some of that, but I see Altman as mainly saying something practical.

If you keep pushing the ‘have the AI do a bunch of these things for you’ buttons, things go faster, but you do not get ‘operational excellence’ and you get an increasing amount of misalignment difficulties. This is probably not because Astra is actively sabotaging you. This is mostly a Skill Issue.

No, This Is Not a Strawman

I am very worried that people will say ‘well you predicted that big dangerous things might happen in 2027 and gave it a 25% chance, but it is now 2028 and it did not happen, so you have been proven wrong and this means nothing will ever happen.’

Seriously, this happens all the time, including straight up.

Tom Chivers: Sure, this guy is predicting AI doom in the next year, but he was predicting AI doom in ten years nine years ago, and it hasn’t happened yet.

There are a bunch of common variations of this. Let [X] be some bad thing.

Here are ten examples of things people often say. Each of these ends ‘therefore you lose all credibility and [X] will never happen.’

  1. You said that by now there was a [10% / 25% / 50%] chance of [X].
  2. You used to say [X] would happen [sooner/later], now you say [later/sooner].
  3. You used to say [X] would happen [more/less] often, now you say [less/more] often.
  4. You mentioned that [Y] might happen before [X], but [Y] hasn’t happened.
  5. You did not sufficiently loudly say that [X] also might not happen.
  6. The market does not predict [X], if [X] was going to happen we would see [Y]. (usually in a way that would make no sense even if the market really did believe it).
  7. If you really believed [X] you would (do a thing that makes no sense and is often morally abominable, or make a trade that makes no sense, etc).
  8. If you really believed [X] you would (do a thing that only makes sense if [X] is 99%+ to happen, which you did not predict.)
  9. If [X] happened that would be weird or bad or surprising or whatever.
  10. [X] would be something happening, whereas we all know nothing ever happens. Or it would require intelligence enabling some new thing we do not currently know how to do, which sounds like science fiction. And so on.

You will continue to see such arguments, usually from people who have continuously made now-falsified predictions about AI. Do not listen to them.

We Need a Plan That Meets the Moment

A lot of evidence is in.

Many things point to the substantial possibility of superintelligence in 2027:

  1. Extrapolation from the AECI and many other metrics of AI capabilities, as per the analysis of the AI Futures Project.
  2. METR’s report from inside Anthropic.
  3. Widespread claims, against interest, both from OpenAI and Anthropic employees as well as many official communications.
  4. The analysis of many who have previously made highly accurate predictions about AI capabilities.
  5. The forecast, in particular, of Paul Christiano.

There are also reasons for skepticism as well. Many remain skeptical. Most reasons for skepticism are ignorance of the evidence, or failure to consider the evidence, but there are also better arguments. I am taking many of those better arguments into consideration, as well as the potential for model error. This is why I continue to believe that the probability of full automation of AI R&D in 2027 is under 50%.

In order to meet this moment, any plan has to be ready for the full automation of AI R&D inside Anthropic or OpenAI, and perhaps beyond that, by the end of 2027, resulting in rapid RSI and advancement in AI capabilities beyond human levels.

The most obvious plan is to slow or pause advancements in AI capabilities. Here is a thread of a few of the people supporting this: Nate Silver, Elizabeth Warren, the Financial Times editorial board, Ezra Klein, Eric Hoel, Robert Wiblin, Rutger Bregman, Peggy Noonan and Abdul El-Sayed.

Any plan that works on that time frame needs to include mechanisms to slow down the resulting growth in capabilities. We also need to be as ready as we can for when and if those capabilities arrive, including what happens if that development goes well. We would then face a host of other urgent and deadly problems.

The plan also cannot assume that this will happen. We cannot stop planning for futures in which AI capabilities only advance a smaller amount without anything we could call a takeoff.

And also, yes, we need to be ready for the possibility that radical improvement in AI capabilities might not upend things as much as I expect that they would, or do so as fast as I would expect that to happen. We could still blow the ‘easy’ worlds.

We cannot and must not burn our seed corn, of any type, until and unless we get much stronger evidence, either personally or globally, that we are in a world where we need to do that. It’s a marathon, folks. Until it isn’t.

item.title: I am not making time to grieve
item.description:
There sure has been a lot of bad news lately.[1]

(This is not a post about epistemics, or AI doom arguments, or making a case for any specific beliefs. It's been written about plenty and I'm not going to spend the time it would take to do it justice. This post takes for granted that, while I have high uncertainty and I obviously hope that we're enormously wrong about the risks of AI, I am taking it seriously, and it's scary.)

It feels like it's been a long time coming. I've been reading Lesswrong for, like, half my life? In 2015, after years of agonizing, I left ICU nursing, the job of my dreams, that I'd been working toward since I was fourteen, because some people whose opinions I respected made sufficiently compelling arguments that the world was in trouble, and that maybe my contribution could matter.

I think they weren't wrong. It sure seems like it matters now. I mean, it still feels arrogant to say so, but here I am, working 50 hours a week on those grounds, missing precious moments of my daughter's childhood and spending obscene amounts of money on childcare, and nobody has actually made the case to me that I'm wrong about that calculation.

Less than a year ago, at the Berkeley 2025 Solstice, I gave the following speech.

To my daughter Iomedae

In a week you’ll be twenty months old. I don’t know what you think of this whole existence. You don’t yet have the words to tell me. But I know that you smile easily. You like sauerkraut and olives and kale stew. You charm strangers in airports. In September you swam in the ocean, fearlessly, shrieking with joy in the waves.

I think you’re happy, most of the time. I know that you’re perfect in every way and I love you more than anything. 

At night when you’re asleep, I fret about keeping up at work. About our right to be in this country. Things keep happening on the news, and I don’t like them. I’m terrified for the future of the world, and most of the time it’s too big to look at, but it’s always there in the background. 

But in the morning you wake me with your sweet babble, and reach for me with your little arms, and it’s good, and perfect, and nothing can take that away from me. 

I want you to get to live forever. I want to see you grow up and be so incredibly cool, and I want to be proud of whatever it is you do, and I want you to have all the resources I can offer you to be whoever you want to be. 

I don’t know if you get to live to be ten. 

I wish I could protect you; I wish I could fix everything for you. I do what I can, or at least I try. It’s not very much, though I do take some personal pride in the beautifully organized state of Lighthaven’s finances. Even if I knew all the right things to do, which I don’t, I’ve learned the hard way that I can’t just use willpower to be some other person with personality traits better suited to the work at hand. Your glorious perfection doesn’t, actually, make me perfect. 

Sometimes I worry it was selfish to have you. I’ve wanted a child since I was sixteen years old, and having a baby to fill your unmet emotional needs raises some red flags. Sometimes my Internet friends debate whether it’s ethical to bring a person into the world at all, when you can’t ask their consent beforehand and they might well end up wishing you hadn’t. 

And yet most parents from history would look at our house and see wealth and opportunity beyond wonder. On the larger stage, events happen at a terrifying and unprecedented speed and I feel like the world stopped making sense sometime in my late 20s, but I shift my focus to look at our street, our village, and - it’s good. 

I didn’t get to ask your permission, but I chose this. I chose you, wholeheartedly, and I want to savor every second. I want to drink in every perfect moment that, no matter what the future holds, can’t be unmade. To siphon off a little of that joy, every day, filling up a secret reservoir that had been drained for years before I had you in my life. I tell myself that having you makes me stronger, and maybe, if someday I need to do something very very hard because one can make an argument that it’s the right thing to do and I’m the best person to do it, maybe I can draw on that strength. 

I think you’re happy, most of the time. I know that I love you more than anything, and tomorrow you’ll wake me with your sweet babble, and that moment will be good and right and perfect and nothing will ever take that away.

If someday I need to do something very very hard because one can make an argument that it’s the right thing to do and I’m the best person to do it, maybe I can draw on that strength. 

If, I said.

I didn't expect that 'if' to arrive before the next Solstice.

I am not okay with this. I am not resigned. But I've already done a lot of processing.

I was depressed for years. I had suicidal thoughts over my feelings of inadequacy at how poor a job I was doing at fixing the world's biggest problems, and at the same time I missed ICU nursing and bitterly resented leaving. I have crammed such an unbelievable quantity of angst about not wanting to be ambitious into the last decade. I did my processing and my grieving over years, mostly via writing my own 1.7 million word take on a Mercedes Lackey fantasy trilogy from the 90s about it[2].

I learned about a cancer diagnosis, and stared at the various 5-year mortality rates, and that was all the way back in 2020. Then I went into journalism, and got to spend a year with it being literally my job to read all the most deeply upsetting news. I processed my angst into a sprawling set of wish-fulfillment stories where my self-insert got to do all the shiny ICU medicine in an actually functional healthcare system, in an actually functional world, never needing to worry about whether she should be doing something more important[3].

I spent nearly a decade desperately wanting a baby, however conflicted I thought I was supposed to feel about the cost to my career or the ethics of bringing a child into such an uncertain world. I wrote a story about being the daughter whose mother knew she lived in a doomed world, and had her anyway.

Before any of that, I was an ICU nurse. I watched human beings die, in front of me, enough times that I no longer remember exactly how many.[4]

I gave a different Solstice speech about it once.

Last November, I went out for breakfast with a colleague after our last night shift. It had been an awful night for her–struggling to keep her patient alive till the morning, the inexperienced resident scared shitless, every nurse on the unit hanging around the room staring at the monitor.

The patient died at 7:45 am. My colleague finished charting, and we went out and ate a huge greasy diner breakfast and drank endless decaf coffee, and we told all our most horrific stories, and we laughed. Yeah. We laughed.

And one of the things that really makes it sink in, how many problems there are in the world, is that learning to laugh at the horror is one hundred percent necessary. It’s maybe one of the healthiest coping mechanisms, healthier than alcohol or even greasy diner breakfasts. It was the best way I knew to take what I saw at work, and somehow accept it and then move on.

So I gave up my day’s sleep to sit with my colleague and friend, and laugh so we could postpone the tears. Later I cried. And it was right, to feel sad for the person who just died, who was someone’s mother, someone’s sister, someone’s friend. I wanted to grieve, even if she wasn’t my family, even if I knew next to nothing aside from her name and age.

We stood outside the patient’s room at 7:45 am, exhausted after 12 hours, and watched her heart rate drop farther and farther until it was just an occasional ventricular beat. Watched the blood pressure go down to 30/10, which at that point is not really a blood pressure anymore, before we lost it entirely. She had a do-not-resuscitate order, and was already maxed on every vasopressor and we were running epinephrine at five times the supposed maximum dose, and we knew there was no winning this one–we had known it for days, really. You can’t save them all.

It’s been over a year, and I can still see that scene perfectly in my head. I don’t remember all of my patients, by any stretch of the imagination. But I remember the ones we couldn’t save.

I had a lady once for five 12-hour shifts. She had advanced chronic lung disease; she had been on home oxygen for years; and she was back in the ICU for the second time that year, on a ventilator, sedated. Her friend and maybe-lover came to see her every day, and sat by her bedside to talk to her, and asked me if I knew when she’d be coming back so he could get her room ready. It was one of the sweetest things I had ever seen.

She was my ‘boring’ patient that week. She got maybe a third of my time. I strained my back trying to turn her alone. Once I left her in a soiled bed for hours before I could find a second nurse to help me clean her. I put dressings on her inevitable bedsores, and I tried to make sure she wasn’t in pain.

Maybe three weeks later, I had two other patients and was run off my feet and stopped midafternoon at the nursing station, and I saw that her heart rate was 30. I glanced over, and knew immediately that she was palliative, that they were going to take her off the ventilator and switch her to comfort care only.

I didn’t have time to watch; she wasn’t my patient. But I did anyway, stood outside the room where she was alone, and watched her heart stop, and I wanted to say, I’m sorry. I’m sorry I called you my boring patient. I’m sorry I didn’t love you more. Fellow human, I want you to know that I know this is wrong, even though it’s the least wrong option. That for the last ten years you were slowly losing your strength, tethered to your oxygen, and the last three weeks of your life were spent helpless in a bed, surrounded by beeping machines, and that now there’s nothing more we can offer you except for a death without pain… We gave you our best, every step of the way, but that doesn’t make it right. I’m sorry that humans still have to get old and die. I’m sorry that I didn’t have the courage to go into the room with you and hold your hand, because you weren’t my patient and it would’ve looked weird and I didn’t have time.

The memory is hazy now. I’ve forgotten her name. I can’t even wrap my head around the tragedy of that one death. And we lose two more people every second. We’ve lost another sixty million since her. Gone, just like that. We can’t save them all. And we can’t take the time to grieve for them the way we ought to – so we laugh, and look away, and keep moving forward.

Because one thing I know is that we can’t afford to stop.

I am not okay about the world or its future, and I am not resigned, and I don't think it makes sense for me, right now, to make time to grieve it, when I have done so much fucking grieving already.

To start with: what time, exactly? I have a job! I have a toddler! I have a ridiculous supernatural medical drama novel I'm not finished editing. I have Wednesday night neighborhood dinners to pick up cooking for again whenever I can manage it.

I don't think I've ever been any good at sitting down on purpose to deliberately process grief anyway. It's hard to imagine an amount of staring that would get me to, what, acceptance? Of the fact that my child may not live long enough to start kindergarten? I wrote a Solstice speech for that one too. For most of history, that was what mothers could expect for half of their children. It was an upbeat speech, but I cried writing it[5]. I made my unhappiest self-insert deal with a lot worse.

And grieving the possible extinction of humanity, not just 'someday, but maybe, conceivably, as soon as next year...

Nope. I'm too busy. I mostly feel very little temptation to spend my limited free time on doomscrolling, and I don't think it's worth re-opening the trapdoor to the bottomless pit of this-isn't-what-I-wanted just to stare at it, when I could stare at pictures of my beautiful perfect child instead.

I do intend to try to leave myself time to decompress, because it wouldn't be very strategic of me to disastrously burn out in the next month. I'll make allowances and be gentle with myself when I inevitably end up angsting until 3 am, and I will grieve, whether or not I plan time for it. That's fine.

I am absolutely going to take every moment I have left, every moment I can squeeze into every day, to love my daughter. I could have died of cancer in 2021, and she would never have existed. Every perfect moment we have is one that didn't have to happen.

I still wouldn't call myself ambitious. I still have the same old worn-out angst that maybe if I was worse at things, I wouldn't have quite so many things to do, and I could pick the ones that exult my soul without abandoning more important responsibilities. But I've managed to grow some very specific ambitions. I'd like the accounting done right. Sounds like a nice support-role sidekick project, right? Well, I work for Oliver Habryka, so I think it's going to take some ambition to pull it off.

I think my daughter is happy, most of the time. Deciding to have her is one thing I don't feel conflicted about at all.[6] I want her to have a world to grow up in, and there are tasks in front of me that might help.

    I was originally going to go find ten links to recent news for each word in this sentence, and concluded that another thing I don't feel like making time for right now is going back and rereading depressing blog posts.

  2. ^

    On the topic of processing via fictional analogies: in book 11 of A Song for Two Voices, the Existential Bad Outcome that the characters have been staring down for twenty years very abruptly escalates, things start happening relentlessly, and the rest plays out over roughly a month. Lately I catch myself wondering how I'll know when I'm in this timeline's Book 11. I don't think we're in book 11 of ASFTV quite yet, but I'm not 100% sure we aren't, and it feels like I maybe just didn't think to write the version of book 11 where it felt hard to be sure if it was really that serious and also it might play out over multiple years. Anyway: hi there, Final Books Of ASFTV Feeling. It's nice to have a shared reference for you.

  3. ^

    I started to write a version of this sentence including 'and no one ever tells her she needs to be more ambitious', before remembering that that's completely false.

  4. ^

    I once attended a CFAR retreat on grieving, and oh my god was that a terrible mistake when I had a shift back in the trauma ICU in Reno the next day.

Sure, it takes time to parent her, but I waste so much less time on being sad at my lack of BABY. Also, she's objectively perfect in every way, and this includes being pretty easy to parent.

item.title: Basic Problems With the Chip Security Act
item.description:
Epistemic status: I have no experience in law or anything, I just read this bill and noticed some issues. This is not deeply researched.

[Crossposted from my blog, BlueprintingHeaven.]

Here is my attempt at preventing these problems from being overlooked. I am not a US citizen, so if you are, please do what I cannot.

Briefly, the Chip Security Act is about making sure chips aren't getting smuggled into places they're not supposed to be. A mix of ping-based location verification, inspections, and other things is proposed. It is currently being negotiated as part of the annual defence bill, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which basically always gets passed. The final text is expected to be released this December.

I am looking at the version passed by the House Foreign Affairs Committee in March 2026.

Issue number one is the inspections are listed as "periodic". Issue number two is the super long timeframes given for some requirements, some of them longer than my AI timelines.

Periodic inspections are mentioned here:

The term ‘‘chip security mechanism’’ means a software-, firmware-, or hardware-enabled security mechanism or a physical security mechanism, including—
(A) periodic on-site audits or inventories at the end-user’s approved destination for the covered integrated circuit product;

(Note that inspections are optional: they're one choice of ~4, and as long as one of them is done, that counts. Which one is done is decided by Commerce. Ping-based location verification is another example of an option.) The word periodic does not necessarily imply inspections with regular time intervals, but it's certainly not strict enough to imply random inspections. Inspections have to be random, or very short notice, otherwise the entities being inspected can move incriminating objects off-site before the auditors arrive. This is super basic and obvious and it's what you do for nuclear inspections![1]

The Chip Security Act has timeframes that are far too long. The May 2025 version had shorter timeframes; I assume industry pressure (mainly from the Semiconductor Industry Association) extended them. The lengths of time given are ceilings though, so once the bill passes (I think it's probably too late to get the timeframe adjusted but I'd love to be proven wrong), Commerce should be pressured to move way, way faster than the deadlines.

What long timeframes am I talking about?

Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of State, the Secretary of Defense, and the Secretary of Energy, shall require any covered integrated circuit product that is exported, reexported, or in-country transferred to or within a foreign country to be secured by a chip security mechanism that enables reliable verification of whether the product has been illegally diverted to destinations of concern, to the maximum extent practicable, using techniques that are feasible and appropriate on such date of enactment.

The above paragraph can be crudely summarised as "chips must have security mechanisms one year after the Act is enacted". This used to be 180 days in the May 2025 version. I think this is the most important one. Implementing basic chip security mechanisms in December 2027? I don't know if we'd survive.

If any enhanced chip security mechanisms identified pursuant to paragraph (1)(A) are determined by the Secretary to be appropriate, the Secretary may, not later than two years after the date on which the Secretary completes the assessment required by paragraph (1), require any covered integrated circuit product to incorporate the enhanced chip security mechanisms, or for additional mechanisms to be otherwise implemented, at the time the product is exported, reexported, or in-country transferred to or in a foreign country.

This basically says if there are some chip mechanisms that seem good to implement, the Secretary has two years to require chips to incorporate those security mechanisms after they complete the assessment. In the May 2025 version, the assessment itself was due one year after enactment; now it's due two years after it. (It also used to say "shall" (as in, must) instead of "may".) So in the worst case scenario, improved security mechanisms might not be required until about four years after the Act is passed.

Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary, in robust consultation with the public in a manner determined appropriate by the Secretary and in consultation with the heads of other relevant Federal departments and agencies, shall promulgate a final rule that includes a reporting requirement to inform the Bureau of Industry and Security of the Department of Commerce whenever chip security mechanisms fail to confirm that any covered integrated circuit product has not been illegally diverted to a destination of concern, taking into account reasonable time for persons to verify or repair the chip security mechanism, identified in the final rule, including instances in which there is evidence that a product has been subjected to tampering or an attempt at tampering, including efforts to disable, spoof, falsify, manipulate, mislead, or circumvent chip security mechanisms.

This reporting of diversion or tampering was originally meant to be set up in 180 days, not one year.

Those are the basic problems I noticed. If you’re a US citizen, please contact your representative and senators and ask them to press Commerce to implement the Chip Security Act well ahead of its legal deadlines. You can find your representatives at congress.gov/members.

One final note: Section 6(c) lets Commerce keep a record of the location and end-user of every exported advanced chip, but it's optional. This should not be optional, because those records could prove super useful for treaty verification later (and would be useful for current enforcement, as in the stuff the Chip Security Act is trying to accomplish).
